The web interface works through a REST API that b4 serves on the web server's port, under /api/. The API reference on this site lists every endpoint with its parameters and responses. With the address of a running b4 in its B4 Instance field, that page sends its requests to that instance; without one, it only shows the reference.

While a username and a password are set under Settings > System > Web Server, every request under /api/ needs a login token, except those to /api/auth/ and /api/version. Without a username and password, no token is needed. Step Request Log in POST /api/auth/login with {"username": "...", "password": "..."} returns {"token": "..."} Use the token An Authorization: Bearer <token> header on every request. WebSocket connections under /api/ws/ can pass it as the token query parameter instead Log out POST /api/auth/logout revokes the token A login token stays valid while it is used at least once every 24 hours, and is discarded when b4 restarts. After repeated failed logins from one address, b4 answers 429 for a while. The MCP endpoint has a token of its own, see MCP server.

Request What it does GET /api/metrics The dashboard snapshot GET /api/metrics/summary A short summary of the snapshot, with the connection totals since the last counter reset /api/ws/metrics WebSocket: a full snapshot, then one update per second, as the dashboard receives them POST /api/metrics/reset Reset counters on the dashboard POST /api/escalations/clear Clear on the dashboard's Active Escalations panel: every escalated host goes back to its set GET /api/ipbans The banned addresses the dashboard's Banned addresses panel lists POST /api/ipbans/clear Unban on that panel with {"key": "<address>:<port>"}, or Clear all without a key /api/ws/logs WebSocket: the live log the Logs page shows POST /api/logs/trace/start, POST /api/logs/trace/stop Start trace and Stop & save on the Logs page GET /api/logs/trace/status Whether a trace is recording GET /api/logs/trace/download The last trace file, as Download last trace saves it GET /api/config/download The configuration as it is, as Download as is under Settings > System > Backup saves it GET /api/config/download?safe=true The safe copy, as Download safe copy saves it GET /api/system/addresses The ports the Expose to internet switches opened, their firewall chains and errors, and the reason a switch that is on opened nothing GET /api/watchdog/status The watchdog's state for every watched set and domain, with the reason codes POST /api/discovery/start Starts a Discovery run. A run for a set that routes its traffic is refused with 400 and the code routed_set, and any run while b4 is still applying its DSCP rules with 409 and the code dscp_rules_pending POST /api/discovery/replace, POST /api/discovery/add, POST /api/sets/{id}/add-domain with tested Write a Discovery result into a set, create a set from it, or add its domains to a set. With the run's dscp_path, a set whose traffic takes another DSCP path is refused with 409 and the code dscp_path_changed, and a write while b4 is still applying its DSCP rules with dscp_rules_pending POST /api/mcp The MCP server, see below

The watchdog reports why a set is in its state, or how its last heal ended, as one of these codes. The Watchdog page shows the same reasons in words. Code Meaning not_owned The set's addresses are handled by another set or by none, so a strategy written into this set does not affect them escalated An escalation sends the addresses to another set unusable A certificate error, a required client certificate, or a private or local destination. Never healed current_works Tested alone, the set's own strategy loads the addresses, yet the live check fails not_needed Tested alone, the addresses load without a bypass, yet the live check fails partial The search found a strategy for only some of the addresses, so nothing was written none The search found no working strategy incomplete The search ended without a confirmed result budget The search ran longer than 20 minutes and was canceled start_failed The Discovery run could not start verify_failed The strategy written did not pass the live check and was undone edited The set was changed during the check or the search, so nothing was written busy Another Discovery run holds the runtime, and the heal waits rules_changed b4 was applying or rewriting the firewall rules the search depends on, such as its DSCP rules, so nothing was written; the heal is tried again later

For an Expose to internet switch that is on but opened nothing, GET /api/system/addresses gives the reason as one of no_auth, web_no_auth, open_relay, shared_port, loopback, invalid_bind and not_listening. Securing the web interface describes the conditions of each switch.

POST /api/mcp serves the Model Context Protocol to AI applications, as JSON-RPC 2.0 over HTTP. Connecting an AI assistant covers the setup. Only POST is served: GET and DELETE return 405, which is normal for this transport. Situation Response Enable MCP server is off 404, mcp server is disabled An MCP token is set, and the request carries none or another one 401, invalid or missing MCP token No MCP token is set The web interface's login token is required, as for the rest of the API, while a username and password are set The request carries an Origin header that is not allowed 403 A request with an Origin header is accepted when that origin is b4's own address written as an IP address or localhost, or is listed in system.web_server.mcp.allowed_origins, where a single * accepts any origin. A host name is never accepted automatically: under DNS rebinding, a page on an attacker's name reaches b4 with matching Origin and Host headers. AI applications send no Origin header.

The server offers tools according to the two permission switches on the MCP server card and rebuilds the list when they change, without a restart. An application that was connected before the change keeps its old list until it reconnects. A tool that is not permitted is not offered at all, and the server tells the model which permission is off, so the model can say what to turn on. Permitted Tools offered Nothing (default) 14 Allow configuration changes 18 Allow active probes 16 Both 20 Tool What it does Needs b4_status Version, capture engine, firewall backend, how many sets exist and are enabled, the state of Telegram over WebSocket, uptime, the connections counted since the last counter reset, and which permissions are on - b4_metrics Connections in the last complete minute, in sets and not in a set, the totals since the last reset, dropped resets, blocked DNS lookups and connections, b4's CPU and memory use. Connections count as on the dashboard - b4_get_config The configuration, or one section of it - b4_list_sets Every set in priority order, with domain counts and primary strategy - b4_get_set One set in full - b4_check_domain Which sets target a domain, how the match was made, and whether the set is enabled - b4_recent_connections Connections b4 processed, with the set that matched each - b4_logs_tail The tail of errors.log, or of update.log with file=update - b4_diagnostics OS, kernel, interfaces, firewall backend and the rule groups b4 installed - b4_get_topic The description of a setting, see Topics - b4_list_writable_paths Which settings can be changed, with types, current values and accepted values - b4_geo_lookup Which GeoSite and GeoIP categories exist, what one holds, and which cover a domain or an address - b4_api_reference The REST API's operations, or one of them with its parameters, body and responses, see below - b4_watchdog The watchdog's verdicts, and its actions, see below Depends on the action b4_set_config_value Changes one setting and applies it at once, reporting the previous and the new value Allow configuration changes b4_revert_last_change Restores the configuration from before the last change made over MCP Allow configuration changes b4_edit_set_targets Adds or removes domains, addresses, geo categories, ASNs or source devices of one set Allow configuration changes b4_manage_set Creates, duplicates, moves, enables, deletes or resets a set Allow configuration changes b4_test_domain_now Fetches a domain through b4 and again with b4 bypassed, and says which of the two works Allow active probes b4_find_bypass_strategy Runs Discovery for a domain, a URL or a set, and applies the result Allow active probes to start a run, Allow configuration changes to apply it b4_check_domain answers whether a domain is configured in a set. b4_recent_connections answers whether traffic for it arrived and which set matched. The difference separates a targeting mistake from a routing one. A ready-made prompt, diagnose_domain, comes with the tools. It takes a domain and walks the model through the status, the coverage, the configuration and the firewall rules, in that order. Applications that support prompts list it separately.

Reading the watchdog's verdicts emits no traffic and changes nothing, so the tool is offered at every level, and each action is permitted on its own. Without set, the actions work on the older per-domain list and the global watchdog switch: Action Effect Needs status The last verdict for every watched set and domain - add Adds a domain to the list Allow configuration changes and Allow active probes remove Removes a domain from the list Allow configuration changes enable Turns the global watchdog switch on, for the watched sets and the list Allow configuration changes and Allow active probes disable Turns the global watchdog switch off Allow configuration changes check Checks a domain of the list now Allow active probes With set, a set id or exact name, the actions work on that set's own watchdog and its Discovery addresses, passed as url: Action with set Effect Needs status The set's watchdog status, reason and per-address results - enable Switches the set's watchdog on and schedules a check; refused when the set cannot be watched Allow configuration changes and Allow active probes disable Switches the set's watchdog off Allow configuration changes add Adds url to the set's Discovery addresses Allow configuration changes and Allow active probes remove Removes url from them Allow configuration changes check Schedules a check of every address of a watched set and clears its cooldown Allow active probes; a give-up is cleared only when Allow configuration changes is on as well

domains takes up to five domains or full URLs, separated by commas, as the Discovery input does: a domain is fetched as https://<domain>/, a URL as given. A host that only serves files, such as an image or video CDN, can answer / with HTTP 400 and leave the run nothing to test. Such a host is probed by the URL of a file it serves. A run also tries the strategies the community hub publishes for the domains, as a run from the Discovery page does when the hub is on. action=start with set runs Discovery for that set: on the domains given, or on the set's Discovery addresses, at most five. The set's current strategy is tested first, and the search stops at the first strategy confirmed on every address. action=status reports the verdict, and action=apply with set writes the result into the set, the strategy only and only for the verdict covered. The same applies to action=apply without set when the run it refers to was a run for a set. A set that action=apply creates for free-form domains keeps the addresses they were found on as its Discovery addresses. A set with routing enabled is refused, and so is a result whose probes took another DSCP path than the set's traffic takes now, as on the Discovery page.

With Allow configuration changes on, these become writable: every setting inside a set: targets, fragmentation, faking, TCP and UDP, DNS, escalation and routing; the MTProto and SOCKS5 settings, the Telegram over WebSocket switch system.mtproto.bridge.enabled among them; the logging settings, so the model can raise the log level, reproduce a problem and read the result. b4_list_writable_paths reports the exact paths with their types, current values and accepted values. A change goes through the same validation and live-apply path as a save in the web interface. An invalid result is rejected and nothing is saved, and an accepted one applies at once, firewall rules included. Writing a list, such as a set's domains, replaces the whole list, so a model reads the current value first and sends it back in full. b4_edit_set_targets adds and removes single entries instead, with kind naming the list: sni_domains, ip, geosite_categories, geoip_categories, asns or source_devices. An asns entry is written as AS15169 or 15169 and stored as the bare number; reserved numbers are refused. An ASN whose prefixes b4 has not fetched yet is added anyway and fetched at once, and the reply names it, because until the fetch succeeds the set matches none of its addresses. Whatever the switches say, the credentials of the web interface, SOCKS5, MTProto and a set's upstream proxy are refused, and so are these: Refused Reason Web server settings Moving or locking the interface removes the way to undo the change The MCP settings The model cannot widen its own permissions Capture engine and TUN Switching it under a live network can cut the machine off Firewall backend A wrong value leaves the machine with no rules at all Every Expose to internet switch, and any write that would open a port while one of them is on, such as turning the MTProto proxy on or changing its port An open port is reachable from the whole internet at once, and a revert does not undo what reached it Packet marks and routing tables b4's own traffic depends on them Set DSCP (system.tables.dscp) and a set's own DSCP (sets[].dscp) Rules on the next router act on the value, and a wrong one can send traffic down another route A set's id Escalation targets refer to it A set's Discovery addresses and watchdog switch Both make the router fetch sites on a timer; b4_watchdog with set changes them under its own permissions The log directory and the geodata file locations A wrong log directory silently stops file logging, and a wrong geodata path empties every category at once The dividing line is recoverability: a wrong value inside a set breaks some sites, visibly and reversibly, while a wrong web server port or capture engine can leave the machine unreachable. The writable areas are named as whole subtrees, and the exclusions are marked on the fields themselves, so a setting added to b4 later stays unwritable until it is opted in. Refusing a location does not refuse the contents: b4_logs_tail reads both log files wherever the directory points. b4_revert_last_change restores the configuration from before the most recent change made over MCP since b4 started, and applies it. Repeating it walks further back. It is refused, and the change stays on the list, when the configuration changed after that change, by a watchdog heal, the web interface or another tool. It is also refused when it would switch a set's watchdog or the global watchdog on, or bring back watched domains or the Discovery addresses of a watched set, while Allow active probes is off.

Several b4 settings have names that read as something other than what they do, and a zero usually means "use the fixed value" rather than "off". b4 carries a written description of such settings, and the server tells the model to read it before explaining or changing anything. The descriptions come from src/ai/topics.json, built into the binary; the web interface's AI explanations use the same text. The descriptions are published twice: the tool b4_get_topic, with topic for an exact key, path for the setting a b4_set_config_value path names (in sets[video].tcp.win.mode the set is ignored), or query for a search. With no arguments it lists every documented key; the resources b4://topics/<key>, with the same text. Most applications never show resources to the model; LM Studio and the OpenAI-compatible bridges list them for the user. The tool makes the text reachable for the model. A question about a setting without a description returns a note saying so, with the documented settings nearby. The note tells the model to say it is unsure rather than guess the setting's unit, default or meaning from its name.

The tool gives the model the reference that the API reference page shows, from a copy built into b4 that matches the installed version. It covers what the other tools leave out, and the model makes the API calls itself. The tool only describes the API. Arguments Answer None Every operation, by tag query The operations whose path, summary or description contain every word given operation, as PUT /api/sets/{id} The operation's parameters, request body and responses, with the types they use. A path with a real value, such as /api/sets/abc123, names the same operation schema One type from an earlier answer, with its fields A type too large for one answer is listed by name, for a later call with schema. An operation that another tool also performs names that tool. A REST write passes b4's own validation, but not the checks and refusals that the MCP tools add. Apart from schema, each answer also explains how to call the API. While a username and a password are set, that is the login, and the model is told to ask the user before using them. The MCP token is refused outside /api/mcp.

Every tool call writes one line to b4's log, shown on the Logs page: the tool, the caller's address and how long it took. A refused call is logged as a warning. A request turned away at the endpoint is logged too: the server off, a wrong or missing token, or a browser origin that is not allowed. The token itself is never written. Repeated refusals are collapsed into one line every 30 seconds, with a count. These lines go to the live log and the console, not to errors.log, which holds errors only. A change made or reverted over MCP also appears under Recent changes on the dashboard as AI agent changed a setting, with the path of the setting and without its value.

Tool output may be forwarded to a third-party model, so b4 removes these values from it or replaces them with [redacted]: the username and password of the web interface; the MCP token; the SOCKS5 username and password; the names and values of the MTProto secrets; the IPinfo token; the reference to the stored AI API key; the username and password of a set's upstream proxy; the path of the web server's TLS key. Host names and URLs are returned as configured. Download safe copy under Settings > System > Backup masks those as well. b4_diagnostics holds no credentials, but it reports the hostname, every interface address and the live firewall ruleset, which is enough to identify the network.

b4 accepts command-line flags, and they take precedence over the values in the configuration file. A flag overrides the setting for one run only. When b4 saves its configuration, a setting that came from a flag keeps the value the file already had.

Flag Description Default --config Path to the configuration file Discovered, /etc/b4/b4.json on most systems --verbose Log level: debug, trace, info, silent info -v, --version Print the version and exit - --clear-tables Remove b4's iptables/nftables rules and exit -

Flag Description Setting Default --queue-num The first netfilter queue number queue.start_num 537 --threads Number of worker threads queue.threads 4 --mark The queue mark, see Packet marks queue.mark 32768 --ipv4 Process IPv4 traffic queue.ipv4 true --ipv6 Process IPv6 traffic queue.ipv6 false --ipv6 is the Enable IPv6 Support switch under Settings > Core > Packet Engine. It decides whether b4 processes IPv6, not whether the router uses it. With it off, IPv6 connections pass the router without any set applying to them. In NFQUEUE mode, sets with Remove ECH keys from DNS answers on still remove ECH keys from IPv6 DNS answers. See The queue section.

Flag Description Setting Default --skip-tables Do not create iptables/nftables rules at startup system.tables.skip_setup false --tables-monitor-interval How often to check and restore the rules, in seconds. With NFQUEUE 0 turns the check off; in TUN mode the interval is at least 10, and 0 does not turn it off system.tables.monitor_interval 10

Flag Description Setting Default -i, --instaflush Flush log writes immediately system.logging.instaflush true --syslog Send log lines to syslog as well system.logging.syslog false --log-dir Directory for b4's log files. Empty turns file logging off system.logging.directory /var/log/b4
Flag Description Setting Default --web-port Port of the web interface. 0 turns it off system.web_server.port 7000

Variable Description Setting GOMEMLIMIT The memory limit of the Go runtime. While it is set, b4 does not apply Memory Limit system.memory_limit GOMEMLIMIT takes the Go runtime's format, not the field's: a byte count such as 268435456 or 256MiB, or off. With a value such as 256m, b4 does not start.

A custom configuration file and debug logging: b4 --config /opt/etc/b4/b4.json --verbose debug Removing b4's firewall rules: b4 --clear-tables Running without automatic firewall setup, with the rules managed by hand: b4 --skip-tables IPv6 processing for this run only, with the configuration file left as it is: b4 --ipv6
b4 keeps its configuration in one JSON file, /etc/b4/b4.json by default. The --config flag points it elsewhere.

Platform Path Linux /etc/b4/b4.json OpenWRT (with extroot or USB storage) /opt/etc/b4/b4.json OpenWRT (without USB storage) /etc/b4/b4.json ASUS Merlin /opt/etc/b4/b4.json Keenetic /opt/etc/b4/b4.json Docker /etc/b4/b4.json, inside the container Without --config, b4 looks for b4.json and config.json under /etc/b4 and /opt/etc/b4, and falls back to /etc/b4/b4.json. The log names the path it settled on at startup. The Download Configuration card under Settings > System > Backup saves the configuration in the form b4 writes to this file. Its safe copy masks credentials and private host names for sharing, and b4 refuses to load or save a configuration that still holds the safe copy's [redacted] placeholders.

The file is sparse. A setting that holds its built-in default is left out, so a fresh installation writes a very short file, and a section whose settings were never changed is absent. A missing key is not a missing setting, and adding it back with its default value changes nothing. Saves from the web interface, the API and MCP write the file the same way.
documents.s: Only what differs from the defaults is stored

documents.t: { "version": 52, "queue": { "start_num": 537, "threads": 4, "mark": 32768, "ipv4": true, "ipv6": false, "tcp_conn_bytes_limit": 19, "udp_conn_bytes_limit": 8, "interfaces": [], "mss_clamp": { "enabled": false, "size": 88 }, "devices": { "enabled": false, "vendor_lookup": false } }, "system": { "tables": { "skip_setup": false, "monitor_interval": 10, "engine": "", "masquerade": { "enabled": false, "interfaces": [] }, "dscp": { "enabled": false, "value": 0, "interfaces": [] } }, "logging": { "level": 1, "directory": "/var/log/b4", "instaflush": true, "syslog": false }, "web_server": { "port": 7000, "bind_address": "0.0.0.0", "expose": false, "tls_cert": "", "tls_key": "", "username": "", "password": "", "language": "en", "mcp": { "enabled": false, "allow_writes": false } }, "dns": { "tcp_disabled": false, "tcp_port": 5453, "query_timeout_sec": 5, "keep_ipv6_answers": false }, "socks5": { "enabled": false, "port": 1080, "bind_address": "0.0.0.0", "expose": false, "allowed_sources": ["192.168.1.0/24", "127.0.0.1/32"] }, "mtproto": { "enabled": false, "port": 3128, "bind_address": "0.0.0.0", "expose": false }, "checker": { "discovery_timeout": 5, "config_propagate_ms": 1500, "dns_server": "" }, "geo": { "sitedat_path": "", "ipdat_path": "", "sitedat_url": "", "ipdat_url": "" }, "timezone": "" }, "sets": [] } The sample shows some of the sections and some of their keys. A real file holds only the keys that differ from the default. system.mtproto.secrets is a list of named secrets, each with id, name, secret and enabled. A file written before configuration version 50 held a single mtproto.secret string, which the migration moves into the list as an entry named default. system.socks5.allowed_sources is absent while the list is empty, the default, and the proxy then accepts any source. Each entry is an IP address or a CIDR range. 0.0.0.0/0, ::/0 and malformed entries are refused when the file is loaded or saved.

Key Meaning Default start_num The first NFQUEUE number 537 threads Number of worker threads 4 mark The queue mark, see Packet marks 32768 ipv4 Process IPv4 traffic true ipv6 Process IPv6 traffic false tcp_conn_bytes_limit How many packets at the start of a TCP connection b4 inspects 19 udp_conn_bytes_limit The same for UDP 8 interfaces Capture Interfaces, a filter on the interface a packet passes. Empty means all of them [] tcp_conn_bytes_limit and udp_conn_bytes_limit apply to every set. A set's own tcp.conn_bytes_limit and udp.conn_bytes_limit have no effect, and the web interface has no field for them. queue.ipv6 decides whether b4 processes IPv6, not whether the router uses it. Off, the default, b4 processes IPv4 only and writes no IPv6 firewall rules for any set, so a client that reaches a site over IPv6 bypasses the sets. b4 then removes IPv6 addresses from DNS answers for the domains sets match, see DNS. The exception is NFQUEUE mode while an enabled set has dns.strip_ech on. In that mode b4 writes IPv6 rules for DNS answers and DNS over TCP, only to remove their ECH keys. A change takes full effect after a restart. --ipv6 sets the same thing for one run.

Each set is one object in the sets array, carrying its whole configuration. Its keys follow the tabs of the set editor: targets - domains, IPs, GeoSite and GeoIP categories, ASNs, source devices tcp - general TCP settings, desync, window, incoming, RST protection fragmentation - the fragmentation method and its parameters faking - SNI faking, SYN fakes, mutation udp - the QUIC filter, the port filter, the handling of calls and the UDP action mode dns - the set's resolver, DoH URL and pins routing - routing mode, output interface, upstream proxy or blocking dscp - the set's own DSCP value discovery - the set's Discovery addresses and its watchdog switch escalate - which set to escalate to when this one stops working The Import/Export tab of the set editor shows a set as JSON and takes a pasted one back. The exported JSON leaves out values equal to the defaults and the settings of switched-off features. It also leaves out the set's id, source devices, watchdog switch and escalation settings, and, when the set has source devices, its dscp.

Key Meaning Default dscp.enabled Enable per-set DSCP: write the set's own value into the packets to the set's addresses, see DSCP false dscp.value The value written into the DSCP field, 0-63. 0 clears the field 0 Each key is stored only while it differs from its default: the switch on with the value 0 is saved as "dscp": {"enabled": true}, a value kept with the switch off as "dscp": {"value": 12}. While dscp.enabled is true, a dscp.value outside 0-63 is refused, not clamped: the web interface refuses the save, and a file that holds one stops b4 at start. Neither key is writable over MCP or carried in a shared set.

Calls on a set's UDP tab is stored in two keys, see Sets for calls. Calls Stored as Pass call setup udp.filter_stun is true, the default Handle like other UDP udp.filter_stun is false Handle only calls udp.filter_l7 lists the calls of Which calls: ["discord", "stun"] for Discord app and browsers, ["discord"] for Discord app, ["stun"] for Browsers A non-empty udp.filter_l7 means Handle only calls whatever udp.filter_stun holds, and udp.filter_stun then has no effect. An empty list is not stored. A set with the list needs a udp.dport_filter, no targets.sni_domains, targets.ip, targets.geosite_categories, targets.geoip_categories or targets.asns, and an empty tcp.dport_filter. A set that breaks this is refused: the web interface refuses the save, and a file that holds one stops b4 at start. An escalate.to that names a set with the list is cleared, with a warning in the log. An unknown entry stays in the list, matches no traffic and is logged as a warning. (auto: STUN request) is "fake_payload_file": "@stun" under udp. udp.filter_l7 is writable over MCP, with discord and stun as its only entries, and is carried in a shared set.
documents.s: A set's calls: udp.filter_stun and udp.filter_l7

These settings exist only in the file. Path What it does Default system.web_server.mcp.allowed_origins Browser origins the MCP endpoint accepts besides b4's own address. A single * accepts any origin Empty system.checker.watchdog.heal_validation_tries The number of fetches in a row a strategy has to pass during a heal's search 3 system.checker.watchdog.verify_tries The number of tries each address gets in the check after a heal writes a strategy 2 system.checker.discovery_flow_mark, system.checker.discovery_injected_mark The marks of Discovery's test traffic, see Packet marks The queue mark plus 1 and plus 2 queue.tun.route_table A fixed routing table for the TUN engine instead of a free one b4 picks, see Packet marks Picked by b4 sets[].routing.fwmark, sets[].routing.table A pinned mark and table for a set that routes traffic, used only when both are set, see Packet marks Picked by b4

version at the top is the configuration format version. b4 reads it to decide what needs migrating, so it stays unchanged when anything else is edited. warning The values in the file are checked only when b4 starts, and a file that fails the check stops b4 with an invalid configuration error. b4 reads the file only at start, so a manual edit takes effect after a restart. Any save before then writes the running configuration over the file, and the manual edit is lost. Saves come from the web interface, MCP, a watchdog heal, a geodata download and an ASN prefix update.

When the format changes between releases, b4 migrates the file at startup: new fields arrive with their defaults, and renamed ones are carried over. Before it changes anything, it writes a backup next to the file, named after the version it migrates from, for example b4.json.v51.bak. A file that cannot be read at startup, for example one cut short by a power loss or left with a JSON syntax error, is copied next to itself as b4.json.corrupt. When an earlier copy with different content is there, the name is b4.json.corrupt.1 and onward. The log names the copy. b4 then starts on the defaults, and the next save replaces the original file, so the unreadable settings remain only in that copy. A file whose version is higher than the running binary understands is loaded as it is, with a warning. Settings that binary does not know are dropped at the next save.

TSPU (Technical Means of Countering Threats, ТСПУ) is the Russian deep packet inspection (DPI) system installed in internet providers' networks. It is the system that blocks access to sites and services.

A detailed technical description of the TSPU (ASBI) architecture, its components, how it works and how it filters is kept in a separate project: tspu-docs - a guide in 24 chapters, based on a lecture of about five hours on the architecture, configuration and operation of TSPU. The material is in Russian. Accuracy The documentation was generated with AI from the lecture transcript and checked by hand. It may be out of date: TSPU is updated continuously, and the current implementation can differ from the one described. Inaccuracies are possible. Main topics: The ASBI/TSPU architecture: balancers, filters, the DPI engine Blocking methods: DNS spoofing, SNI filtering, IP blocking Detection: how TSPU recognises bypass attempts Weak points: what b4's bypass strategies rely on Knowing how TSPU works helps when choosing and tuning bypass strategies. It is not needed for everyday use of b4: Discovery finds a working configuration automatically.

b4 downloads its releases, the installer and the GeoSite and GeoIP databases from GitHub. On some networks the host that serves the release files, release-assets.githubusercontent.com, is blocked, and an update stops with a connection timeout. There are three ways around it: mirrors, a personal Cloudflare Worker, and installing from a file.
documents.s: Downloading b4 when GitHub is blocked

documents.t: b4 tries GitHub first, then each mirror in Update mirrors, then the mirrors built into b4, then SourceForge. Every source serves the same archive, checked against the same published SHA256. On a network without blocks, the mirrors are never used.

Update mirrors under Settings > System > Service takes a comma-separated list of mirror addresses. They are tried before the built-in mirrors, and b4 passes them to the installer, so an update from the web interface uses them too. Only https addresses are accepted. An entry with a query string or a fragment is ignored. A mirror that works on one network can be blocked on another, because each provider blocks on its own. A list of several mirrors is tried in order. A mirror serves the binary that becomes b4 b4 checks every download against the SHA256 published next to it, but the checksum comes from the same host as the archive. A host that serves both can serve a matching pair. Only mirrors under one's own control, or trusted ones, belong in this field.

A Cloudflare Worker is a free mirror on a personal Cloudflare account, under a *.workers.dev name. It fetches from GitHub inside Cloudflare's network and passes the result on. Every account gets its own subdomain, so there is no single name to block. On some networks *.workers.dev names are throttled: small responses get through, while an archive crawls. b4 abandons a stalled download and moves on to the next source. The checks below show whether a Worker is usable from a given network. A Worker bound to a custom domain is not affected. This Worker is not the Cloudflare Worker relay for Telegram, which runs a different script.

Create a free Cloudflare account. Under Compute > Workers & Pages, create a Worker from the default template and deploy it. Replace the Worker's code with the script below and deploy again. In b4, add the Worker's address, such as https://name-1234.username.workers.dev, to Update mirrors under Settings > System > Service.

const REPO_OWNER = "DanielLavrushin"; const REPO_NAME = "b4"; const MIRROR_OWNERS = [ "DanielLavrushin", "Loyalsoldier", "runetfreedom", "XTLS", "Flowseal", ]; const MIRROR_HOSTS = [ "raw.githubusercontent.com", "github.com", "api.github.com", "objects.githubusercontent.com", "release-assets.githubusercontent.com", "codeload.github.com", "gist.githubusercontent.com", ]; const SF_BASE = "https://downloads.sourceforge.net/project/b4core"; const SEGMENT = /^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._+-]*$/; const RAW_PATH = /^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._/+-]*$/; const API_TTL = 300; function text(body, status) { return new Response(body, { status, headers: { "content-type": "text/plain; charset=utf-8" }, }); } function allowed(raw) { let url; try { url = new URL(raw); } catch { return false; } if (url.protocol !== "https:") return false; if (!MIRROR_HOSTS.includes(url.hostname)) return false; const parts = url.pathname.split("/").filter(Boolean); const owner = parts[0] === "repos" ? parts[1] : parts[0]; return MIRROR_OWNERS.includes(owner); } async function passthrough(request, target, ttl) { const headers = new Headers(); const range = request.headers.get("range"); if (range) headers.set("range", range); headers.set("accept-encoding", "identity"); headers.set("user-agent", "b4-mirror"); if (target.startsWith("https://api.github.com")) { headers.set("accept", "application/vnd.github+json"); } const init = { method: request.method === "HEAD" ? "HEAD" : "GET", headers, redirect: "follow", }; if (!range && ttl) init.cf = { cacheTtl: ttl, cacheEverything: true }; let upstream; try { upstream = await fetch(target, init); } catch (err) { return text(`upstream fetch failed: ${err}
`, 502); } const out = new Headers(); for (const name of [ "content-type", "content-length", "content-range", "accept-ranges", "etag", "last-modified", ]) { const value = upstream.headers.get(name); if (value) out.set(name, value); } out.set("access-control-allow-origin", "*"); return new Response(upstream.body, { status: upstream.status, headers: out }); } export default { async fetch(request) { const url = new URL(request.url); const path = url.pathname; if (request.method !== "GET" && request.method !== "HEAD") { return text("method not allowed
", 405); } if (path === "/b4/health") return text("ok
", 200); let m = path.match(/^/b4/dl/latest/(.+)$/); if (m) { if (!SEGMENT.test(m[1])) return text("bad file name
", 404); return passthrough( request, `https://github.com/${REPO_OWNER}/${REPO_NAME}/releases/latest/download/${m[1]}`, 0, ); } m = path.match(/^/b4/dl/([^/]+)/(.+)$/); if (m) { if (!SEGMENT.test(m[1]) || !SEGMENT.test(m[2])) { return text("bad tag or file name
", 404); } return passthrough( request, `https://github.com/${REPO_OWNER}/${REPO_NAME}/releases/download/${m[1]}/${m[2]}`, 0, ); } m = path.match(/^/b4/sf/([^/]+)/(.+)$/); if (m) { if (!SEGMENT.test(m[1]) || !SEGMENT.test(m[2])) { return text("bad tag or file name
", 404); } return passthrough(request, `${SF_BASE}/${m[1]}/${m[2]}`, 0); } m = path.match(/^/b4/raw/(.+)$/); if (m) { if (!RAW_PATH.test(m[1])) return text("bad path
", 404); return passthrough( request, `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/${REPO_OWNER}/${REPO_NAME}/${m[1]}`, API_TTL, ); } if (path === "/b4/api/releases") { return passthrough( request, `https://api.github.com/repos/${REPO_OWNER}/${REPO_NAME}/releases?per_page=25`, API_TTL, ); } if (path === "/b4/api/releases/latest") { return passthrough( request, `https://api.github.com/repos/${REPO_OWNER}/${REPO_NAME}/releases/latest`, API_TTL, ); } if (path.startsWith("/github/")) { const target = url.href.slice(url.origin.length + "/github/".length); if (!allowed(target)) return text("forbidden
", 403); return passthrough(request, target, 0); } return text("not found
", 404); }, }; The script fetches only from GitHub and SourceForge, and only for the repository owners it lists, so it cannot serve as an open proxy. Release archives pass through it without being cached.

curl -sI https://name-1234.username.workers.dev/b4/health curl -sL -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{size_download}\n' \ https://name-1234.username.workers.dev/b4/dl/latest/b4-linux-arm64.tar.gz The first command checks that the Worker answers. The second downloads a release archive through it and prints the status and the size. A download that stalls here means workers.dev is throttled on this network.

When no source can be reached, the archive can be brought in by hand, from a machine that has access. Requirements: A username and a password for the web interface, under Settings > System > Web Server. Without them the upload is refused, since it replaces the binary that runs as root. b4 running as a service, not in Docker. The installer script. b4 fetches install.sh, or uses the copy it saved at its last successful update. A router that has never been updated from the web interface needs install.sh reachable. Steps: Open the Version Management dialog from the version at the bottom of the side menu. Click Install from a file instead. On a machine with access, download b4-linux-<arch>.tar.gz for the router's architecture from the release page. The dialog links to it on GitHub, and SourceForge mirror opens the same release on SourceForge, with the same archives and .sha256 files. Click Choose archive and pick the file. Optionally, paste the SHA256 from the release page into Expected SHA256 (optional). Click Install. Before anything is replaced, b4 checks that the archive holds a b4 binary for this router's architecture, and refuses one built for another. The SHA256 read on the release page, on another machine, is an independent check of the upload. Hard-float and soft-float MIPS builds pass the architecture check alike, so on MIPS the archive name has to match the router, such as mipsle_softfloat. A wrong one is rolled back after the swap, as is any new binary that does not run.

The installer tries the sources in the same order and reads B4_MIRRORS from the environment. A mirror then works for a first install too, before b4 has any settings: B4_MIRRORS="https://name-1234.username.workers.dev" sh install.sh The value is a space-separated list. B4_SF_BASE replaces the SourceForge address the same way. When raw.githubusercontent.com is blocked as well, the Worker serves the installer itself: curl -fsSL https://name-1234.username.workers.dev/b4/raw/main/install.sh -o install.sh

ADDED: Connections to an address the provider blocks for all sites on it fail at once instead of hanging - sets with IP Block Detection and Cache Blocked IPs on ban such an address for 24 hours, or for 7 days when it is caught again. DNS answers that list other addresses leave it out, and the dashboard's Banned addresses panel lists the bans. Bans are on by default, and Remember blocked addresses under Settings, Core, Packet Engine turns them off. The saved ban list with re-tests is inspired by Ladon. ADDED: AI apps connected to b4's MCP server can look up b4's REST API - the b4_api_reference tool describes every operation of that API from a copy built into b4, for tasks the other MCP tools do not cover. With a login set for the web interface, calls to the API need its username and password. The tool tells the AI app to ask the user for them first. CHANGED: The MTProto proxy's first answer to a Telegram app follows the answer of its Fake SNI Domain - b4 checks that site from the router every few hours and copies its cipher, its key exchange and the size of the first part of its answer. The answer also carries a real encryption key instead of random bytes and comes after a short pause. A site without TLS 1.3 cannot be followed, and the log warns about it. FIXED: In TUN mode b4 could keep the router's processor fully busy, and sites stopped opening on every device - b4 learned which device a connection came from by reading the router's whole list of connections. On some routers one read takes about a quarter of a second, and b4 did one for nearly every new connection. Since 1.88.0 it also did one for every DNS answer the router sends a device. FIXED: On Keenetic, connections to port 443 through a proxy set or Telegram over WebSocket stalled once they opened - Telegram, for example, stayed on Updating. Keenetic's firewall drops data that arrives for port 443 on the router itself, apart from its own. These sets hand their connections to b4 on the router, and that rule dropped their data. #469, thanks @asovetov FIXED: Sites that need a bypass could stop loading until b4 was restarted - this happened when the firmware or another service removed the firewall rules that pass traffic to b4 but left the rest of b4's rules. b4 checks its rules regularly, but these were not part of the check and were never put back. #468, thanks @asovetov FIXED: With Telegram over WebSocket on, proxy sets never got the Telegram connections the bridge cannot relay itself - the switch takes every connection to Telegram's addresses ahead of other sets. Such connections, a bot's requests to api.telegram.org for example, went through the Cloudflare Worker or directly, even when a proxy set listed the site or covered Telegram's addresses. Where Telegram's addresses are blocked, they were reset after about 13 seconds. FIXED: Photos and videos through the MTProto proxy or Telegram over WebSocket sometimes started loading only after 1-3 seconds - b4 sent each media connection of a Telegram app through Telegram's own WebSocket server or a Cloudflare relay, whichever answered. The two led to different Telegram servers, and the app's key for media worked only on the side that made it. Each switch made the app create a new key, and its other new connections waited for it. FIXED: On some networks Telegram over WebSocket and the MTProto proxy stopped loading photos, videos and files - b4 opened each connection through Cloudflare, to the shared domains or a Cloudflare Worker, with a first message too large for one network packet. Since late October some networks drop such connections to Cloudflare. Where Telegram's own servers were reachable, messages still went through, but everything that needs a Cloudflare route timed out.

FIXED: On Keenetic, devices handled by Device Filtering could not open any site, even one in no set - Keenetic lets a connection out under the router's address only after its own firewall rules have marked it. b4 took the first packets of these connections before those rules ran. The connections then left with the device's local address and got no answer. #466 FIXED: With Device Filtering on, b4 could rebuild its firewall rules every 10 seconds - a rule from the firmware or another service that b4's own iptables could not read hid one of b4's rules from its checks. b4 took that rule for missing and rebuilt all of them each time. Each rebuild ran dozens of firewall commands, and saving settings waited for it. FIXED: The log showed four failed routing commands each time the Telegram over WebSocket set was rebuilt or removed - b4 tried to remove a QUIC rule chain that such a set never has. A proxy set with Route UDP through upstream on gave the same warnings. They appeared on settings saves that rebuild such a set and on every stop of b4.

FIXED: Some AI apps could not work with b4's MCP server - LM Studio, also through LobeHub, refused every request because five tools without arguments, such as b4_status, lacked a field it requires. With Allow active probes on, apps using OpenAI's API refused every request too, because one tool description was longer than that API accepts. Gemini CLI adds an argument of its own to tool calls, and b4 refused those calls. FIXED: b4_check_domain told AI apps that a domain was covered when a set listed only one of its subdomains - an ad-blocking set that lists ads.youtube.com made youtube.com look covered, so an AI app could decide that nothing needed adding. A link or a host with a port was reported as not covered instead of being checked by its host. A very long name kept the router's processor busy for minutes, in the web interface's domain checks as well. FIXED: Other MCP tools gave AI apps wrong information - b4_recent_connections named its columns wrongly and said that an empty answer meant no traffic since b4 started, though it keeps only the last 500 events. b4_logs_tail called every line of the error log an error and could return older lines from the rotated log while skipping newer ones. The setting descriptions that AI apps read through b4_get_topic got some modes wrong, for example they called every SNI mutation mode compatible with real servers. FIXED: Settings changed through MCP could behave differently from what the AI app was told - a set switched on with b4_set_config_value matched nothing until b4 restarted. A port filter added to a set without targets, or the removal of its last target, made the set act on every connection on its ports, and the reply did not say so. Out-of-range numbers and unknown option values were saved and reported as applied, and some of these numbers could stop b4. FIXED: MCP permission checks had gaps - a write waiting behind another one was still saved after Allow configuration changes was turned off. An AI app could move a SOCKS5 server without a password from 127.0.0.1 to a network address, and could point the addresses b4 fetches its Telegram server lists from at any address, local ones included. The tool hints told AI apps that b4_find_bypass_strategy changes nothing, although its apply action rewrites sets. FIXED: Copy JSON copied a set as dozens of lines, too long for a chat message - in 1.88.0 the copy took the formatted text of the Set Configuration JSON box. Copy JSON in Discovery's Apply as a set dialog copied the set formatted too.

ADDED: A set can handle only calls, such as Discord voice calls - the option is Handle only calls in the Calls field on a set's UDP tab, and Which calls can narrow it to the Discord app or to browsers. Such a set has no targets and acts only on the packet that opens each call on its UDP ports, taking the call from any other set. The guide Discord voice calls describes the setup, and such sets also come from the import tool or the Community Hub. ADDED: The dashboard lists devices again, in its Devices panel - a row shows a device's name and address, how many connections it made and the sites it connects to most. Clicking a device opens its traffic on the Traffic page, its connections through proxy sets and b4's SOCKS5 server included. A device whose MAC address b4 does not know, such as the router itself, is listed by its IP address. ADDED: Devices that left the network can be forgotten under Settings, Core, Devices - an offline device has a Forget device icon next to its name, and Forget offline clears them all at once. b4 deletes the name, selection and MSS value it keeps for the device and removes it from the source devices of sets. A device name can also be removed by saving it empty. ADDED: Settings and the set editor mark unsaved changes and ask before they are lost - a dot marks each changed field and the tab, section or list item that holds it. Leaving the page with unsaved changes, or Discard Changes, first lists each change with its old and new value. In the set editor, Discard Changes takes the place of Cancel and does not close the editor. #434, thanks @alle-ox ADDED: A slider's value can be typed in - clicking the number next to a slider opens a box for it. Enter or a click elsewhere applies the value, and Escape cancels. #434, thanks @alle-ox ADDED: For a site that needs no bypass, Discovery lists the strategies that also loaded it, and any of them can be applied as a set - this helps when a browser still cannot open a site that Discovery's checks load without b4. They appear under N other strategies worked, on the site's result card and in its history row. #423 CHANGED: Filter STUN Packets on a set's UDP tab became the Calls field - on became Pass call setup, and off became Handle like other UDP. With Pass call setup, the set lets STUN requests and the Discord app's voice packets through unchanged. The rest of a call, such as browser audio and video, still gets the set's Action Mode. CHANGED: A set acts on QUIC to an address it learned only when the connection carries a site name the set targets - it also acted on every QUIC connection to such an address, including connections to other sites that share it, such as a CDN address. On the Traffic page the set appears only on the packets of such a connection that carry the name. QUIC Matching set to By SNI or matched destination, on the set's UDP tab, keeps the old behaviour, and UDP that is not QUIC still follows a learned address. #437 CHANGED: The Traffic page and the dashboard show a device by its name, or by its IP address when it has none - the Traffic page used device names only with Enable Device Filtering or Vendor Lookup on. Otherwise it showed most devices by MAC address, and some of a device's connections apart, under its IP address. The MAC address shows on hover and in the Detail pane. CHANGED: A set's JSON pasted on the Import/Export tab is no longer imported at once - it appears formatted in the box, and Import applies it. The box shows where a broken JSON fails, and Format JSON tidies text typed by hand. #434, thanks @alle-ox CHANGED: A Device Filtering change takes effect when the settings are saved, with no restart - the change used to wait for a restart of b4. Before that restart, turning the filter on or off could make b4 process the same connections twice. FIXED: The Traffic page showed STUN and Discord voice packets as handled by a set that let them through - with Filter STUN Packets on, a set passed these packets through unchanged, yet their rows looked the same as rows of packets the set had handled. FIXED: Some set editor help texts described the wrong behaviour - the TCP Port Filter said port 443 is always included, and the UDP Port Filter said an empty field turns it off. A list limits the set to the ports listed, and an empty field means every port. The UDP Evasion Technique said None sends fakes unchanged and TTL lets them expire, while UDP fakes always use the set's Fake TTL. FIXED: The Connection Packets Limit sliders on a set's TCP and UDP tabs had no effect - b4 took the limit for every set from TCP Connection Packets Limit and UDP Connection Packets Limit under Settings, Core, Packet Engine. FIXED: The import tool lost a port filter or the shared domains without a warning - a zapret port range with equal or reversed ends, such as 3478-3478, was dropped when the set was saved. A set whose port filter held only that range acted on every port. Shared domains went unused when every profile had a host list of its own. FIXED: Site tests reported sites that redirect to their www. address, such as youtube.com and wikipedia.org, as failing both with and without b4 - the MCP tool b4_test_domain_now and the Test button of a Community Hub set stopped at any redirect to another host, even one of the same site. If a site sent visitors on to another site, such as twitter.com to x.com, or answered with a nearly empty page, b4_test_domain_now also said the address may be blocked or the site may be down. #445 FIXED: MCP answers did not tell an AI app which setting to change, or where - a refused write read only "Configuration is invalid". Messages about Allow active probes and Allow configuration changes did not say that these switches are in b4's web interface. An AI app then sent users to its own settings. #446 FIXED: An MCP undo that needed Allow active probes stayed refused after the switch was turned on - b4 counted the switch itself as a newer change to the configuration and refused the undo as outdated. FIXED: A block set limited to Source Interfaces also blocked other interfaces and the router itself - only blocking by address followed the list. Blocking by name, in DNS lookups and in connections, applied to every device and to the router's own connections. A block set with an escalation target also stopped blocking a site once a device retried a blocked connection a few times. FIXED: Block QUIC (force TCP) had no effect on a proxy set with Route UDP through upstream on - b4 sent all of the set's UDP, QUIC included, to the upstream before the switch could act. Over a slow upstream, such as one behind a TCP-only VPN, videos then loaded slowly. With Route UDP through upstream off, QUIC was refused, but the set's other UDP left directly, including the WebRTC requests that can reveal the real address. #456 FIXED: On ASUS routers with Asuswrt-Merlin, a proxy set with Route UDP through upstream off did not refuse QUIC - the router's firewall accepted the devices' traffic before it reached b4's rule. QUIC to the set's addresses left directly, around the upstream. FIXED: On ASUS routers with AiProtection on, and for the devices KeeneticOS lists for its hotspot, b4 missed the replies of many device connections - the firmware writes connection marks of its own. When such a mark held every bit of b4's Packet Mark, b4 took the connection for one of its own lookups. It then saw none of the connection's SYN-ACKs, resets or answers from DNS servers outside the router. #441 FIXED: A proxy set with All devices except selected under Source Devices refused QUIC from the excluded devices too - the set refuses QUIC when Route UDP through upstream is off, and that refusal ignored the device list. FIXED: With the UDP action Coalesce QUIC Initial, an app that opens a QUIC connection in a single packet could not connect at all, even to sites the network does not block - servers such as Cloudflare's and Google's leave a packet that begins with b4's padding packet unanswered, and b4 put the padding packet in front of every repeat the app sent. Browsers were not affected: they open a connection with two packets, and only one of them carries the site name. #427 FIXED: b4 could stop on a malformed QUIC packet sent to an address a set covers - the packet's header declared a longer start than the packet carried. b4 read past the end of the packet while preparing the set's fake packets, and this reached every version that sends them. FIXED: A site a set drops, rejects or blocks over QUIC still opened when another set had learned its address - on an address shared by several sites, such as a CDN address, b4 took both the set and the site name from what the other set had learned for that address, and never read the name the connection itself carried. #437 FIXED: In TUN mode, memory use grew with every new connection - b4 kept a record of where each connection came from and never removed old records. FIXED: On a phone the set editor's Cancel and Save buttons covered the set name, and long section headers were cut off - the buttons shared a row with the name field, which cannot shrink below its minimum width. Section headers were held to one line, so a header wider than its card ran past the edge. Russian headers, being longer, hit it first. #448, #449 FIXED: In the Russian interface the units on sliders and the name of a new set stayed in English - sliders read bytes, ms and sec, and a new set was named Set 5. In both languages the SYN Fake TTL slider showed its value in milliseconds, although the setting counts hops rather than time. #450 FIXED: Device Filtering ignored the devices added under Manual Devices - such a device got no DPI bypass when selected, and still got it when excluded. A selection made only of such devices applied DPI bypass to every device. The filter matched devices by MAC address alone, and these devices, such as clients of the router's own VPN server, have no MAC address b4 can see. #442 FIXED: In TUN mode, Device Filtering kept the selected devices out of RST Injection Protection and Remove ECH keys from DNS answers - b4 took only the packets these devices sent. Resets and answers from a DNS resolver outside the router come from the server, so they never reached b4. FIXED: A device without a name vanished from the device lists when it went offline, while b4 kept its selection and MSS value - this hit the list under Settings, Core, Devices and a set's Source Devices list. Such a device still counted as selected but could not be seen or unselected on its own. In a set's list, a device whose MAC address was stored in lowercase also showed as not selected. FIXED: Discovery for a set that writes its own DSCP value, and the watchdog's heals of such a set, ran their tests without that value - the tests carried it only to addresses the set had already learned from other traffic. Where a router in front of b4 picks the internet provider by DSCP, the search ran through another provider than the set's traffic. A heal could then write a strategy found there into the set, and applying a result could move its sites into a set with another DSCP value or none. FIXED: b4 kept trying to remove a DSCP chain that was already gone when it ran on iptables and legacy iptables tables also existed - iptables reports a missing chain differently there, and b4 did not read that answer as gone. Its DSCP rules then counted as not applied, and the firewall monitor retried them every few seconds.

ADDED: A set can remove ECH keys from DNS answers, so a browser opens sites such as those on Cloudflare where the network drops connections that use ECH - the switch is under DNS & Routing, DNS Redirect, Encrypted ClientHello (ECH) in the set editor, a set that lists cloudflare-ech.com with it on covers every Cloudflare site, and in NFQUEUE mode it also acts on DNS answers that travel over IPv6 while IPv6 support is off. Discovery proposes such a set, which changes no packets, for a site that loads only without ECH. ADDED: The dashboard warns when a set's TCP port filter makes b4 skip connections - this happens only where b4 tells a device's packets from a server's replies by port. It does so with Skip IPTables/NFTables Setup on or without the kernel's conntrack match. The warning under Recent changes names the ports that cause it. ADDED: System Info shows whether the router holds a dropped QUIC connection, in the row QUIC drop holds for the whole connection - when the router lacks what this needs, the row names it, on OpenWrt the package kmod-nf-conntrack-netlink. ADDED: A set routed through an interface can send its traffic to a gateway on that interface's network, such as a VPN gateway or another router - the field is Gateway (optional) under DNS & Routing, Traffic Routing in the set editor. With an IPv4 gateway on an Ethernet port, bridge, VLAN or Wi-Fi interface, IPv4 devices on that network follow the set too. b4 ignores a gateway outside the interface's network or one of the router's own addresses, and logs why. #401, thanks @alle-ox CHANGED: On Keenetic, and on routers with an older kernel where b4 cannot hold DNS queries ahead of the kernel's connection tracking, DNS queries go on to the resolver the device asked, and b4 takes over that resolver's reply for the names a set blocks, pins or sends to its own resolver - that resolver and the servers it asks still see those names, also for a set with an encrypted resolver. System Info shows the row DNS queries copied, not held (NFLOG). CHANGED: In NFQUEUE mode, a connection that another service sends through a tunnel, or by another route than b4's own packets, gets no strategy from the set it matches - this covers WireGuard, AmneziaWG, TUN and TAP interfaces and, with legacy iptables, connections that a service such as MagiTrickle routes elsewhere by their mark. The Logs page marks them tunnel->wg0 or reroute->ppp1, and block sets still block them. Connections through a tunnel that carries the router's own default route keep their strategies. FIXED: On Keenetic, a device that asked for a name's IPv4 and IPv6 addresses at once, and the router itself, still often lost the second answer after 1.85.1, while System Info showed DNS queries queued before conntrack (raw) as available or the log suggested kmod-ipt-raw, an OpenWrt package - KeeneticOS runs the raw table, where b4 queued DNS queries from 1.85.1 on, only after the kernel's connection tracking has registered them. #402 FIXED: On routers with an older kernel, a device occasionally got only one of the two answers it asked for at once, IPv4 or IPv6, for a name in a set with a DNS redirect - b4 sent both answers at the same moment, and the kernel's connection tracking dropped one of them as a duplicate of the other. FIXED: On routers with iptables and an older kernel, such as Keenetic, connections through a set with SYN Fake Packets on took about a second longer to open, and with the UDP mode Fake & Fragment most of the fakes were lost, often along with the real first QUIC packet - since 1.25.0, b4 put the packets it sends itself through its own queue a second time, and the kernel's connection tracking on such a router dropped some of them. FIXED: A device that sends several DNS lookups from one socket, such as a DNS server on the local network, had its later lookups skip b4 once b4 had answered one of them itself or changed one of its answers, for example by removing the IPv6 addresses - b4's firewall rules marked the device's connection as one of b4's own when b4 sent the device an answer as a packet of its own. FIXED: A set with Domain-only matching on applied only to the start of each connection - the rest of the connection went out without the set's strategy and showed no set on the Traffic page. Where several sets share an address or port, those packets could get another set's strategy instead. b4 picked the set for later packets by address or port, and a domain-only set does not track addresses. #428 FIXED: A set that drops or rejects QUIC, or blocks a site, did not stop a browser such as Chrome from opening the site over QUIC - Chrome sends the start of a QUIC connection in two packets, and b4 reads the site name only from the second. A set with Domain-only matching on dropped only that packet. Other sets dropped only the packets b4 sees at the start of a connection, 8 by default, and the later ones reached the server. #428 FIXED: With the UDP action Coalesce QUIC Initial, sites did not open over QUIC in Chrome - b4 put the padding packet in front of every packet of a connection's QUIC handshake, not only the one that carries the site name. The servers left those packets unanswered. Once the set had learned the site's address, this hit the first packet of the handshake too. #427 FIXED: Discovery reported a site, such as one on Cloudflare, as loading without b4 while Chrome could not open it - its probes never used ECH, which a browser such as Chrome uses for every site that publishes an ECH key and which some networks block. FIXED: Discovery could propose a packet strategy remembered from an earlier run for a site that only needed its DNS answer corrected - a remembered strategy that also loaded the site won over the DNS fix. FIXED: System Info listed tools such as jq, sha256sum and ipset without a version when they were on the USB drive b4 is installed on - b4 asked a tool for its version only when it sat in a standard system directory such as /usr/bin or /opt/bin. FIXED: A regexp: entry listed in two sets, such as a set and its copy made with Duplicate, worked only in the set higher in the list, so when one of them was limited by Source devices, some devices got the wrong set or none for the names that entry matches - b4 kept each pattern only for the first set that listed it. FIXED: A device added by hand by its IPv6 address, typed in another form such as in capitals or with leading zeros, was not recognised when b4 matched its traffic to a set's domains, so a set that selects it under Source devices skipped it and one with All devices except selected applied to it - b4 looked packets up by the standard form of their address, while it kept the device's address as typed. FIXED: Apps that use TCP Fast Open could not open sites through a set with a strategy - such an app puts the start of its secure connection into the packet that opens the connection. b4 split that packet like ordinary data, and every piece opened the connection again with different numbering. The site kept one of them and could not read the start. #431 FIXED: Window Mode sent malformed fake packets on connections that use TCP timestamps, which Linux turns on by default - each fake kept the header length of the original packet but carried only the first part of the header. FIXED: SYN MD5 Signature could send its fake SYN without a usable MD5 option, such as for an app that uses TCP Fast Open - when the real SYN's options left no room, the option was left out. When they ended with an end-of-options marker, it went after that marker, where servers stop reading. A server it reached could take the fake for a real SYN. FIXED: b4 could stop on a malformed TCP packet sent to an address a set covers - the packet's header claimed to be shorter than any TCP header can be. b4 read past the end of the packet while applying the set's strategy. FIXED: A set whose TCP port filter covered the ports devices pick for their own connections, such as 1-65535, made b4 skip some or all TCP connections of every set - b4 told a device's packets from a server's replies by their ports. A device's packet from a port in the filter looked like a reply. #429 FIXED: On the router's own connections and on IPv6 connections without address translation, RST Injection Protection, Incoming Response Bypass and the escalation on Forged resets stopped working once b4 had sent fakes or split segments into a connection - since 1.71.1, b4's firewall rules took such a connection for one of b4's own. The server's packets on it then no longer reached b4. FIXED: The router's own connections showed up twice on the Traffic page, and IP Block Detection could mark their addresses as blocked after fewer unanswered attempts than its thresholds - since 1.26.1, with Device Filtering off, b4 handled every packet the router sent twice on its way out. FIXED: Connections from the internet to a server on the local network behind a port forward failed once a set matched them, such as a set that matches port 443 alone - since 1.22.0, b4 took them for a device's own connections to the internet and applied the set's strategy toward the server. FIXED: On nftables, Global MSS Clamping and the MSS Clamping of a set without source devices did not make devices send smaller packets and did not apply to the router's own connections - since 1.39.1, the clamp came after b4's queue rules, and a packet that went through the queue skipped it. FIXED: On a router whose firmware overwrites b4's connection mark, such as some ASUS models, a forwarded port gave no answer to connections from an address in a set routed through an interface - on such a router b4 marks every packet to the set's addresses. It marked the replies to those connections too, and they left through the set's interface. FIXED: Connections that another service on the router had marked, such as those of devices KeeneticOS lists for its hotspot or those MagiTrickle routes, got no strategy from b4's sets - b4 took those marks for the marks of its own packets, which share a bit with them. (#422, thanks @asovetov; #276)

ADDED: The Discovery page shows a run started through the MCP server or by the watchdog while the page is open, and its history marks such runs - the run appears within five seconds, the history refreshes when it ends, and its history rows read "via MCP" or "via watchdog" under the time of the run. ADDED: Copy JSON in Discovery's Apply as a set dialog copies the proposed set without creating it - in the format of the set editor's Import/Export tab, where it can be imported on another device. ADDED: System Info shows the version of each tool it lists, such as iptables, nft, ipset, curl and wget, next to the tool's name - the version is what the tool itself reports, or the BusyBox version for a tool that is part of BusyBox, and Copy JSON and MCP b4_diagnostics include it as version. ADDED: A set can write its own DSCP value into the packets sent to the set's addresses, so a router in front of b4 can route or prioritise each set's traffic separately - the value takes the place of the Set DSCP value for those packets, also while that switch is off, and covers the set's IP, GeoIP and ASN targets and the addresses b4 learns for the set's domains. The switch is under DNS & Routing, Traffic Routing in the set editor, which also shows when a set cannot use it, such as a proxy or block set. ADDED: The browser tab title names the open page, such as "Traffic - B4", so several b4 tabs can be told apart, where every tab used to read "B4" - the set editor adds the set's name, as in "YouTube - Sets - B4", and Settings adds its open tab. ADDED: The Devices panel on the Traffic page sorts by name by default, or by latest activity or packet count through its sort button, where devices used to swap places whenever one of them sent a packet - by name, devices with a name come first, then devices known only by their MAC address, then sources known only by their IP address, and a selected device stays in the panel after its last packet has fallen out of the period. CHANGED: A device on the dashboard's Blocked panel shows its IP address under its name, with the MAC address on hover - the MAC address used to take that line. CHANGED: The dashboard arranges its panels in rows that always fill the full width, each panel as tall as the tallest one in its row, where panels used to be packed into free spots, which left holes and moved them sideways as lists grew - in Customize, the border between two panels and the minus and plus buttons move width between neighbours, a panel dropped on another joins its row, one dropped between rows gets a row of its own, and the row button splits or joins rows. FIXED: Discovery tried every strategy for minutes on a link that gives an error even without b4, such as the bare address of an image host, then reported that nothing worked, as if the site were blocked - when the site answered "bad request", Discovery blamed a strategy for garbling the request, even on the first try, which uses no strategy. FIXED: Discovery started through the MCP server did worse than the same run from the Discovery page: a link such as a YouTube image link failed with an error on every attempt, and the community hub's strategies were never tried - the server cut the link at a comma inside it, took the rest for a second site and lowercased its path, so the site was asked for a page that does not exist, and it left the hub out of the run. FIXED: On Keenetic, b4 was sometimes not running after a router reboot, with no errors.log, and could also stop when it restarted itself to retry its packet engine - the hook b4 installs for the router's firewall rebuilds sent its re-check signal to any process named b4, and a b4 that had only just started was ended by that signal. #404

FIXED: On routers with an older kernel, a device that asked for a name's IPv4 and IPv6 addresses at once often got no answer to the second question, so apps on it, like a video player on a TV, waited and never connected, and the router's own lookups could stall for seconds - b4 queued each DNS query only after the kernel's connection tracking had registered it, so a second query sent at the same moment from the same socket was dropped as a duplicate of the first while that one waited in b4's queue. CHANGED: With iptables, other services' firewall rules for DNS queries, such as an Xray TPROXY rule or mwan3 and KVAS marks, also apply to the queries b4 has already seen - b4 queues the queries from the raw table, ahead of those rules, where before a query released from its queue skipped the later rules of mangle.

ADDED: Discovery takes a trusted DNS server, set under Settings, Discovery or for a single run, written as 9.9.9.9, 127.0.0.1:53053, tcp://, tcp+udp:// or an https:// DNS-over-HTTPS URL, and tests a site through pinned addresses, given for a run under Pinned addresses or taken from the set the run is for - the server's answers are the reference for the DNS check, a proposed set gets the server as its DNS when a set can use it and keeps the pins, and a site whose name exists but has no address in DNS is reported as such, with a pointer to pinning, rather than as misspelled. The Fallback UDP DNS servers list and the unused Reference domain setting are gone. ADDED: Download Configuration under Settings, System, Backup saves the running configuration as is, or as a safe copy for sharing when asking for help - the safe copy replaces passwords, tokens, user names, the host names of the router and its relays and credentials inside URLs with [redacted], and b4 refuses to load or save a configuration that still holds these placeholders. ADDED: System Info shows how many routing sets are installed and, while installing them fails, the error, when the failure began and when b4 tries again - the Routing Sets row is under Firewall, and the log warns when no firewall tool on the system can install routing at all. CHANGED: The settings are regrouped: the Core tab has sub-tabs for Packet Engine, Devices, Firewall, DNS and SOCKS5, and a new System tab after it holds Service with logging, Web Server and Backup, which replaced the Backup tab - a sub-tab shows a dot while it has unsaved changes and an icon while a change waits for a restart. CHANGED: The dashboard shows connections per minute in and outside sets, what each set matched in the last hour, and the problems that need attention - Device Activity and Domains Not In Any Set gave way to links into the Traffic page, the Runtime figures moved to System Info, and Reset Stats became Reset counters, with a Clear button of its own on Active Escalations. CHANGED: MCP b4_status and b4_metrics and the metrics API count each connection once, so their fields changed - connections_seen, current_cps, current_pps and memory_percent gave way to per-minute connection counts, cpu_percent and rss_bytes, /api/metrics and /api/ws/metrics carry the new dashboard snapshot, and POST /api/escalations/clear clears escalations. FIXED: Dashboard figures misled: Active flows only grew, Throughput counted only the first packets of each connection, Workers always read all active, Uptime started over at Reset Stats, and Domains Not In Any Set stopped taking new domains - b4 counted every inspected packet as a connection, never recorded a connection ending and evicted each new domain once the list was full. FIXED: Reset Stats on the dashboard also sent every escalated site back to the set that had failed for it - the reset cleared b4's escalations along with the counters. FIXED: Discovery for a domain that does not exist, such as a misspelled one, ran through every strategy for minutes, each test failing with DNS resolution failed (no such host) - the run did not tell a name without any address apart from a site that a strategy might still open. FIXED: Discovery reported No bypass needed for a site whose resolver gave it a wrong address when no DNS server it tried answered honestly, could propose a DNS redirect that gave a wrong address too, and applying its result could switch off the set's Fail closed when the resolver is unreachable - the run reached the site through the address DNS over HTTPS gave without carrying that address into the set, took the first DNS-over-HTTPS server with any answer, on a router with a local resolver tested fragmented DNS against that resolver instead of the server, and wrote its own DNS settings, with that switch off, over the set's. FIXED: After a Discovery run, DNS queries over TCP for sets with a DNS redirect went to the original resolver once b4 next rebuilt its firewall rules, until b4 restarted, and while a run was going the Active Escalations list on the dashboard kept emptying - Discovery's own packet queue published its state in place of b4's main queue: a DNS-over-TCP listener that was down and an empty escalation list. FIXED: A set whose DNS redirect pointed at a resolver on another device in the local network made lookups of its names wait out the query timeout whenever that resolver asked its upstream over plain DNS, and with Fail closed when the resolver is unreachable on they ended in SERVFAIL - b4 sent that resolver's own upstream queries for those names back to it. FIXED: Switching Time Zone back to Auto kept the previously selected zone in log timestamps until b4 restarted - b4 reloaded the zone it had set itself instead of the system's. FIXED: A NAT Masquerade interface that was down or renamed disappeared from the card, which then looked as if masquerading covered every interface while it was limited to the missing one - the card listed only the interfaces present at the moment and left out saved ones that were not. FIXED: Set cards gave target counts such as 1 domains and 1 IPs, and in Russian the longer labels in the panel a set card opens from its Target, Split, Fake, Route, DNS and Escalate tabs ran into their values or wrapped onto a second line - the number was always followed by the same word, and the label column had a fixed width that the longer Russian labels did not fit.
