Operator notes attach a name shown in place of the HMAC, a note and a tag. The tag staff is a label only. The tag test stops the key's votes and reports from counting, and leaves its activity out of the statistics. Trust stops counting the key against the per-key daily limits; its sets still wait for a moderator, and the per-network limits still apply. Untrust reverses it.

A ban is a reversible quarantine. From the moment it is set: every new record signed by the key is refused; at the next build, its sets leave the catalogue for the Withheld tab; its votes stop counting, and its reports stop counting toward the automatic hide; its pending versions can be approved only with a second confirmation, and stay out of the catalogue. Nothing is deleted, and Unban restores it all at the next build. The ban dialog counts what is affected, and names the mirrors the key announced. A ban leaves them announced; rejecting them on the Mirrors page takes them off.

Every hub that announced itself as a mirror of this one, pending first, with the key that announced it. Status Meaning pending Waiting for a decision rejected Never announced. The tooltip gives the reason announced Approved and in the manifest joining, leaving Joins or leaves the manifest at the next build kept Failing, and kept in the manifest while no mirror passes its check not announced Approved, and joins the manifest after its next passing check Approve runs a health check at once, and the mirror is listed once one passes. Reject needs a reason, and the mirror is never announced. Remove forgets the mirror, which can then announce itself again. Check now and Check all run the health check on demand, and the tooltip of a failed check names the step that failed. Serves compares the mirror's catalogue with this hub's: current, behind by some builds, stale, or ahead of this hub.
Votes lists every vote with the weight it carries, filtered by kind, ASN or Country. A vote that does not count says why, for example that its key is banned or tagged test.

Votes count per strategy, in three cells: the ASN and the country the hub saw the vote come from, and worldwide. Vote Weight Works +1 Broken -1 The publication itself, as a works vote by the author +1 A vote without a known network, such as one relayed by an approved mirror a quarter of the above A vote from a key first seen less than a week ago a quarter of the above The two reductions multiply. Every vote loses half its weight every two weeks. The score is (works + 1) / (all + 2). A router uses a cell once at least two devices voted in it with a total weight of at least one. The hub also defines capped weights for automated votes from the DPI detector, the watchdog and Discovery, which b4 does not send yet.

Reports is the inbox of complaints. A report is open until a moderator marks it dismissed or handled, and Reopen returns it. Hiding, rejecting, restoring and withdrawing close the open reports of what they touch. A listed version is hidden automatically once three open reports against it come from independent keys and networks. Only reports with a known network count, from keys neither banned nor tagged test. Restoring a version dismisses its open reports, so the count starts again.

The page shows the published files, the mirrors and revoked keys the manifest lists, and Build history: every build, why it ran, its result and what it changed. Operation What it does Build now Builds from the store even when nothing changed Start a new epoch Resets the sequence number. Every router treats the new epoch as newer and downloads the catalogue again Revoke a hub signing key Adds a key id to the list every manifest carries. Routers stop trusting anything signed with it A build that would not be newer than the published catalogue, or than one an approved mirror serves, is refused. That follows a restore from an older backup, and a new epoch publishes it, see Keeping the data. Otherwise, a new epoch only makes every router download again. danger Routers keep a revocation forever. The hub refuses to revoke its own signing key, and revoking the key built into b4 needs a separate confirmation, because it cuts off every router that trusts that key. Revoking names the signing key of a hub or a mirror and reaches every router. Banning names a contributor and affects only this hub.

Statistics shows activity per UTC day, the spread of published scores and where votes come from. Audit log records every action with its time, actor, target, reason and changed fields. The actor is console, password login, command line or automatic.

Six limits apply from the next request: Limit Per Default Shares per key day 5 Votes per key day 20 Reports per key day 20 Mirror announcements per key day 48 New keys per network day 5 Requests per network hour 2000 A day is the UTC day and an hour the clock hour. The counters live in memory and start over when the service restarts. A network is the sender's /24, or /48 for IPv6. A refused record or a duplicate share does not spend the quota. What a router shows at a limit is described under Limits. Saved reasons edits the preset reasons of each decision dialog.

The hub sends a digest of new events to a Telegram chat, a webhook, or both. Telegram needs a bot token and a chat id: a number, or @name of a public channel, with the bot a member of the chat. A webhook needs a URL, https:// or plain http:// to a loopback or private address, and an optional signing secret. B4HUB_TELEGRAM_TOKEN, B4HUB_TELEGRAM_CHAT, B4HUB_WEBHOOK_URL and B4HUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET in the service environment override the console, which then shows the field read-only. Values entered in the console are stored encrypted with a key derived from secret. The events are new sets in the queue, reports, versions hidden by reports, failed builds and new mirrors. New sets and reports are selected until the settings are first saved. The first event after a quiet period goes out at once, and later ones at most once per digest interval: 60 seconds by default, from 30 to 3600. A failed delivery is retried with a growing delay, up to 30 minutes. Send a test checks a saved channel. The webhook receives a POST with a JSON body: { "hub": "https://hub.example", "sent_at": "2026-09-27T12:41:15Z", "counts": { "share": 2, "report": 1 }, "events": [ { "kind": "share", "at": "2026-09-27T12:40:58Z", "set_id": "01J9...", "version": 1, "title": "Example", "author": "70837b639d58b777", "asn": "12389", "country": "RU", "url": "https://hub.example/admin/sets/01J9.../v/1" } ], "more": 0, "console": "https://hub.example/admin/queue" } Every request carries X-B4hub-Timestamp, the Unix time of the send. With a secret set, it also carries X-B4hub-Signature: sha256=<hex>: the HMAC-SHA256, under the secret, of the timestamp, a dot and the raw body. Redirects are not followed, and any status outside 2xx is a failure.

b4hub moderate does from the command line what the console does, with the same checks and audit entries. It opens the database directly while the service runs. Every change leaves a build request that b4hub serve picks up within about 10 seconds. Commands What they do list, approve, reject, hide, restore The queue and the version decisions. A set is named as <id> or <id>/<version>. Several can be given at once, and approve is all or nothing withdraw, reinstate, delete Whole sets. delete needs --confirm <id> ban, unban, trust, untrust Keys, named by their HMAC reports, dismiss-report, resolve-report, reopen-report The report inbox mirrors, approve-mirror, reject-mirror, remove-mirror, check-mirror Mirrors status, builds, epoch, revoke Publishing, the build history, a new epoch, and revoking a hub signing key with --confirm <key_id> audit The audit log Editing a version, key notes and tags, saved reasons, notifications and the limits are in the console only.

A set that works can be published to the Community Hub. Other b4 users find it on their Community page once a moderator approves it. b4 publishes the set as a shared set: the strategy and the targets, without anything tied to this router.

The Community Hub is on, see Switching it on. The set is saved. Unsaved changes are not published. The set was tested on the targets it lists. A domain it was never tried on collects Broken reports. A set that handles only calls has no targets and is tested with a call through it.

Open the set and go to the Import/Export tab. In Share with other b4 users, click Prepare shared set. Read Check before sharing and Left out of the shared set, and correct the set where needed. Click Publish to hub.

Prepare shared set shows what is sent. Check before sharing lists what deserves a second look, such as domains that look private to this network or pins everyone importing the set will use. Left out of the shared set lists every dropped setting with the reason. Routing to a proxy or an interface, device filters, escalation and the DNS server address are always dropped, see What leaves the router. The JSON below, with Copy and Download, hands the set over directly. The hub refuses a set without targets, except one that handles only calls. Such a set is published with its Which calls choice and its UDP ports. The published title is the set's name. The router sends no description, and a moderator can add one on the hub.

The section shows the id the hub gave the set and its status, pending moderation. The set appears in the catalogue, for other users and for this router, once a moderator approves it and the router syncs. There is no notification of the decision. Until then, Open in Community opens Set details with a note that the set is not in the catalogue. The published set is now linked to the hub set, like an applied one: its card on the Sets page shows Community set. A version that a moderator hides later leaves the catalogue, and routers that applied it keep it.

After the strategy of a published set changes, the button reads Publish as new version. Publishing then adds the next version to the same hub set, and routers that applied the previous one see Update to version N. When the original set was published by someone else, the hub creates a new set instead. A publication whose strategy and targets match a version the hub already holds is not stored. The hub names that set, and the upload counts as a Works report for it. For a set that handles only calls, the Which calls choice and the UDP ports count as its targets, both for new versions and for duplicates.

Every record the router sends to the hub is signed with its author key. The hub knows the router by this key: new versions of a set can be published only under the key that published it, and the moderators can trust or ban the key. The catalogue shows an author label derived from the key, never the key itself. The key is created on first use and kept in .hub/ in the configuration directory. A backup made under Settings > System > Backup does not include it. A router restored from a backup starts with a new key, and the hub gives a key it first saw less than a week ago less weight in the scores. Settings > Integrations > Community Hub > Author identity shows the key and two actions: Show recovery code shows the code the key is rebuilt from. Anyone with the code can publish and report as this author, so the code is kept private. Restore from code replaces this router's key with the one the code describes. The sets published under it can then get new versions from this router.

Message Meaning Linked to community set ... nothing to publish. The set is linked to a hub set, and its strategy has not changed since. The hub refused the set: ... The message names the reason, such as a set without targets that does not handle only calls, or the daily limit, see Limits.
The terms below appear throughout the web interface. Each section links to the page that covers it in full.
A set ties a list of targets to what b4 does with their traffic. b4 changes nothing until a set targets sites. Sets are created on the Sets page or from a Discovery result, see Sets.

Targets decide which traffic a set applies to: domains, IP addresses and ranges, GeoSite and GeoIP categories, ASNs and source devices. They are edited on the set's Targets tab, see Targets. How sets match traffic explains which set handles a connection that several sets match.

A strategy is the set of packet changes a bypass set makes, such as splitting a request into pieces or sending fake packets ahead of it. It is configured on the set's TCP and UDP tabs, see TCP. Discovery tests strategies and suggests the one that loaded the sites.

The dashboard shows each set's kind. Enable Routing and Routing mode on the set's DNS & Routing tab decide it. Kind Setting What the set does Bypass Enable Routing off Applies its strategy to its traffic. See Unblocking a site Route Network interface Sends its traffic out through another interface, such as a VPN. See Routing sites through a VPN or another interface Proxy Upstream SOCKS5 proxy or Telegram over WebSocket (built-in) Hands its traffic to a SOCKS5 proxy, or to b4's Telegram bridge. See Sending sites through a SOCKS5 proxy Block Block (blackhole) Stops its traffic, for every device and for the router itself. See Blocking ads and sites A proxy set applies no strategy, and neither does a route set whose interface is a tunnel such as a VPN: the tunnel or the proxy carries the traffic to the site. A set routed to a plain interface, such as a second uplink, keeps its strategy, see Network interface.

Discovery tests b4's strategies against sites that do not open. It turns the strategy that loaded them into a new set, or writes it into an existing one. It is the usual way to make a first set, see First steps and Discovery.

The watchdog fetches a set's pages on a schedule. When they keep failing, it runs Discovery for the set and writes the new strategy into it. It is turned on under Settings > Discovery, and for each set with Keep this set working with the watchdog on the set's Discovery tab. See Watchdog.

Escalation moves a site to a backup set when its own set keeps failing to reach it, and tries the original set again after a while. The backup can use another strategy, a VPN or a proxy. The watchdog repairs a whole set on a schedule, while escalation reacts to the failing connections of one site. It is set up on the set's Escalation tab, see Escalation.

Community sets are sets that other b4 users published to the Community Hub. The Community page lists them, applies one in one step, and collects reports on whether it works. An applied set is a normal set marked Community set. The page appears once Enable Community Hub is on under Settings > Integrations, see Community.

The packet engine is how traffic reaches b4: NFQUEUE, the default, has firewall rules hand packets to b4. TUN interface routes the traffic through a virtual interface instead. It is the alternative on kernels without the NFQUEUE modules. Either way, b4 reads only the first packets of each connection. The engine is chosen under Settings > Core > Packet Engine and changes after a restart, see Packet engine. When the engine does not start, the dashboard shows the error and offers the other engine.

The Traffic page shows the connections b4 inspects as they happen: the protocol, the domain, the destination, the device and the set that matched. It shows whether a site's connections reach a set, and adds domains, addresses and networks to sets. DNS for sets uses it to check DNS. b4 sees only the first packets of each connection, up to the per-connection limits under Settings > Core > Packet Engine. One connection therefore gives several entries, and the packet counts say nothing about speed or volume. DNS queries that match a set appear too, with what b4 did with each, while Log Level is Info or more detailed. A connection that a proxy set sends to its upstream appears once. The page opens in Aggregated mode. Raw feed in the top right corner shows single packets instead.

Packets are grouped by device, protocol and domain, and a packet without a domain by its destination address. The groups build up while the page is open. Leaving the page, switching to Raw feed or clearing starts them over. Column Shows Protocol TCP or UDP Domain The domain from the handshake or (no domain), the TLS version (1.2, 1.3) and the labels. A domain outside every set has a + button, see Adding domains to sets Destination The latest destination address, +N when there were several, and its ASN Set The set matched by domain, and the set matched by IP when it is another one Source The device, see Devices Activity Packets per second over the last minute Packets The number of packets in the group Seen Time since the latest packet A click on a row opens the Detail panel: activity, packet count, the time from the first packet to the last, the source, every destination address of the group and the matched sets. For a domain outside every set it also has Add domain to a set. Providers may block TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 differently, and a set can be limited to one TLS version on its Targets tab.

Control Effect Filter field Keeps the matching rows, see Filter 30s, 1m, 5m, 15m, All Shows the groups with packets within that period. 1m is the default Unmatched only Keeps only the groups no set matched Domains only / All packets See Domains only and all packets Trash can Clear Packets, see Pausing and clearing The dashboard opens this page with Unmatched only on from Domains not in any set on Activity, and with a device selected from Blocked, both with the period at All.

The Devices panel on the left lists the sources seen within the period, with the time since the latest packet, the activity and the packet count. A click on a device limits the list to its groups, and All devices removes the selection. Hide devices collapses the panel. Sort devices orders it By name, the default, By latest activity or By packet count. A device is identified by its MAC address. When the MAC is unknown, as for a device behind another router, the source shows by its IP address. Aliases from the device filtering table are always shown. With device filtering or vendor lookup turned on there, the names of discovered devices are used too, and the router's own addresses show as Router.

Raw feed shows the latest 1000 packets one by one, the newest at the bottom. Column Shows Time The time of the packet Protocol TCP or UDP and the labels Set The set matched by IP, or by domain when no set matched by IP Domain The TLS version and the domain. A domain outside every set has a + button Source The device name, or the source IP address and port Destination The destination address and port, the ASN, and a + button for an address outside every set

Labels mark special cases: next to the domain in Aggregated mode, and next to the protocol in the raw feed and in the Detail panel. Label Meaning dup The packet was duplicated, see Packet duplication ip The destination was found blocked by IP. An outlined label means the address was already in the cache of blocked addresses ban The destination is a banned address, and the connection was reset at once block A block set blocked the packet voice A call packet passed through untouched: by a set with Calls on Pass call setup, or by a set that handles only calls, as a later packet of a call the set took. The packet such a set takes itself carries no voice label and shows that set in the Set column proxy The connection came through b4's SOCKS5 proxy Telegram icon A connection of b4's MTProto proxy, with the secret's name Telegram icon with Telegram bridge A connection relayed by Telegram over WebSocket doh, forward, pin, sinkhole and others What b4 did with a DNS query, see DNS for sets

The switch in the control bar applies to both modes. Mode Shows Domains only Packets with a recognised domain. The default All packets Every inspected packet, also the TCP handshake before the ClientHello, connections without SNI and traffic to addresses that have no name

The filter field works in both modes. + joins conditions, and all of them must hold. ! before a condition excludes what it matches. field:value checks one field. Several conditions on the same field hold when any of them matches. An empty value, such as set:, matches an empty field. A word without a field is looked up in every field. Matching ignores case and looks for a substring. The fields of both modes are protocol, domain, destination, tls, flags, asn and device (also alias). set works only in Aggregated mode, source only in the raw feed. Filter Shows protocol:udp UDP packets domain:youtube Packets with "youtube" in the domain protocol:tcp+!domain:google.com TCP packets, except google.com domains asn:AS13335 Destinations in AS13335 (Cloudflare) whose ASN has been looked up flags:dns DNS queries and what b4 did with them set: Groups that no set matched

The + button next to a domain opens Add Domain to Manual List. Pick the domain or one of its parent domains, listed from the most specific to the broadest. For rr1---sn-ab5l6ne7.googlevideo.com these are the name itself and googlevideo.com. Under Target Set, choose one of the enabled sets, or Create New Set and enter a Set Name. Click Add Domain. A domain in a set covers its subdomains too. A service that serves content from many subdomains, such as YouTube or a CDN, is covered by its parent domain, such as googlevideo.com.

The + button next to a destination address, and in the raw feed a click on the address itself, opens Add to a set. b4 looks up which network announces the address, through RIPEstat. The dialog then shows the address, the announced prefix that covers it and the network, such as AS15169 Google LLC. When several networks announce the prefix, one of them is picked in the dialog. A private address has no network. A failed lookup can be repeated with Retry, and the address can be added either way.
documents.s: Adding addresses and networks to sets

documents.t: Choice What goes into the set Single IP The address alone, as /32, or /128 for IPv6. The default Announced prefix that covers this address The prefix, such as 142.250.0.0/15, when it is known and wider than the address A wider range The address with a mask such as /24 or /16, for IPv6 /64 or /48, saved as its network: 142.250.120.139/24 becomes 142.250.120.0/24 The whole network The ASN itself, see ASN. b4 fetches its prefixes and keeps them up to date daily For the whole network, the dialog shows the ASN's prefix count and roughly how many IPv4 addresses it holds, and warns about a large network as the set editor does. The choice is unavailable when the set already has that ASN. An ASN whose prefixes are not known yet is added anyway, and b4 fetches them in the background. The set is chosen under Target Set, as in the domain dialog, and the confirm button names what is added, such as Add AS15169. With an IPInfo token on the Settings > Integrations tab, Enrich with IPInfo shows the address's hostname, organization and location from ipinfo.io, and the hostname can be added to a set's domains. The DPI Detector opens the same dialog from its hosting and CDN results, with the network of the affected provider already chosen.

The network icon next to a destination address looks up its network without opening the dialog. b4 finds the ASN that announces the address and fetches its prefixes into its ASN cache. Addresses of that network then carry a label such as AS15169 Google LLC, and the asn: filter finds them. Every browser sees the same labels, and the ASNs that sets target label their addresses too. The cross on a label deletes that ASN from the cache. An ASN that a set still targets is not deleted: b4 names the sets that use it, and the label stays.

The round button in the bottom right corner pauses and resumes the stream. While it is paused, new packets are not collected. Clear Packets, the trash can in the control bar, removes the collected packets, groups and devices. The number next to Traffic in the side menu counts the packets that matched a set. A click on Traffic in the menu, or clearing the packets, resets it, and it does not grow while the stream is paused.

The dashboard is the first page of the web interface. It shows whether b4 is running, whether the sets match traffic, and what needs attention. The figures update every second. Some panels appear only when they have something to show, such as Blocked while a block set is enabled.

The strip at the top shows the state of the service. Cell Shows Status Running in normal operation. Engine failed means b4 is up but does not process traffic, see below. Engine How b4 captures traffic, NFQUEUE or TUN, and the number of worker threads. Firewall The firewall b4 works with, iptables or nftables. restored N times means something on the router removed b4's rules and b4 put them back. Some router firmware does this routinely, and it is not an error. Set up externally means Skip IPTables/NFTables Setup is on, so b4 installs no rules of its own. Uptime, b4 RAM, CPU How long b4 has been running and what it uses. Hovering a cell shows the peaks. When the live updates stop, a line under the strip says so and the panels dim. The page reconnects by itself, and Retry reconnects at once. After Session expired - sign in again, Sign in opens the login page.

When the packet engine fails to start, the web interface keeps working, but traffic passes through the router untouched: no set applies. A card under the strip shows the error. b4 retries by itself up to three times, and the card shows when the next retry is. Switch to TUN or Switch to NFQUEUE tries the other capture mode, for example TUN when the kernel lacks the modules NFQUEUE needs. Restart b4 starts again once the cause is fixed, such as a missing kernel module. Engine settings opens Settings > Core > Packet Engine.
documents.s: If the packet engine did not start

documents.t: The list appears only when something needs action, errors first. The link on each line opens the place where the problem is fixed. Message Meaning and action Set X: proxy ... unreachable The proxy of a proxy set does not answer: the proxy server is down, or its address on the set's DNS & Routing tab is wrong. Telegram bridge: ... Telegram over WebSocket cannot work. The message names the cause, and Troubleshooting explains each one. Watchdog checks fail for X Some pages of the set stopped opening. The watchdog keeps checking and searches for a new strategy if the failures continue. The watchdog is looking for a working strategy for X A search for the set is waiting or running. No action is needed. The watchdog cannot check X None of the set's pages can be checked, for example because another set handles them. The second line gives the reason. The watchdog gave up on X; its sites may not open Three attempts in a row to find a new strategy failed, and the watchdog stopped searching for this set. Searches resume after Check now on the Watchdog page, or once a check finds every page loading, for example after a manual Discovery run for the set. The watchdog is off, but N sets ask for it Either the watchdog is turned on under Settings > Discovery, or Keep this set working with the watchdog is turned off in those sets. No packets reached b4 in the last N min While devices are in use, this means their traffic is not reaching b4, and no set applies. The link opens the packet engine settings. No packets reached b4 lists the causes and fixes. SOCKS5 server did not start, MTProto server did not start, Web server error That part of b4 did not start. The second line shows the error, for example a port that another program already uses. Web server TLS is not usable, serving plain HTTP instead The certificate or key under Settings > System > Web Server cannot be used, so the web interface runs over plain HTTP. The second line shows the error. Some set targets could not be loaded Some set targets were not loaded. The second line shows the error, and the link opens Sets. b4 was updated on disk; restart to run it Restart runs the new version. b4 skipped the bypass for N packets, b4's packet queue overflowed b4 could not keep up with the traffic for a moment, and some connections got no bypass. The router's connection table is N% full The router is close to its limit of open connections, and new connections may fail. The limit belongs to the router, not to b4. b4 holds N OS threads b4 uses far more threads than normal and may stop. A restart clears the state. For a bug report, goroutines.txt in the log directory holds the details when file logging is on. IPv6 traffic skips all sets The router has IPv6, but b4 handles only IPv4, so connections over IPv6 skip the sets. Enable IPv6 Support under Settings > Core > Packet Engine brings IPv6 into the sets. In TUN mode the message reads TUN mode does not handle IPv6; IPv6 traffic skips b4, because that mode never handles it. The cross on a start failure or on the IPv6 message hides it.

The chart shows how many connections b4 checked each minute: in your sets when a set matched the connection, not in a set otherwise. 1 h and 24 h switch the time window, and Table shows the same numbers as rows. Live traffic opens the Traffic page. Domains not in any set opens the Traffic page with only the connections no set matched: the sites that are not in a set yet. The history is kept in memory and starts over when b4 restarts.

Each TCP connection or UDP flow counts once, when it starts. b4 sees only the first packets of a connection, so the dashboard does not show how long a connection lasted or how much data it carried. Only connections to the ports b4 watches count: 443 and the ports the sets add. Connections count whether they come from devices on the network or from the router itself, and connections through proxy sets count too. DNS queries, Discovery's test connections and devices that device filtering leaves out do not.

One row for each enabled set. A row shows the set's kind (Bypass, Route, Proxy or Block), how many connections it matched in the last hour, and when it last matched. Proxy sets also show their open connections, and upstream down while their proxy fails. Block sets show how many DNS lookups they blocked. A set's name opens it. When a set shows no matches although its sites are in use, the Traffic page shows which set, if any, their connections get. A set that the watchdog keeps working shows its status: Healthy, Failing, Healing, Gave up, Can't check, Not checked yet or Watchdog off. The status opens the set's Discovery tab.

What happened since b4 started, newest first: starts, applied settings, firewall rules restored, strategies the watchdog switched, settings an AI assistant changed over MCP, warnings and errors. Most entries link to the related page. The list is kept in memory and starts over when b4 restarts. The warning TCP port filters cover the source ports of client connections means that b4 passes some connections unprocessed. A set's TCP port filter covers the ports devices pick for their own connections, and on this router b4 tells a device's packets from the server's by their ports. The second line names the ports. A filter below 32768 avoids it, and When b4 tells the direction by port lists the cases.

Top domains lists the names devices connect to most. Top addresses lists connections without a name, such as Telegram apps, voice calls, games and VPN servers. Badges show the sets that matched. + marks a name or an address that no set matched, and adds the domain, or the address, its network or its ASN, to a set. Both lists count from the last reset.
Shown while a host is moved to a backup set because its own set kept failing, see Escalation. Each row shows the host, the set it moved to and when it goes back. Clear sends every host back at once.
Shown while a block set is enabled. Domains lists what was blocked, Devices the devices that tried to reach it. A device opens its traffic.

Shown while IP block detection has banned addresses. Each row shows the address, the domain and set it was caught on, how many times it was caught and the time left. Unban lifts one ban at once, and Clear all lifts every ban.

Shown while the MTProto proxy or Telegram over WebSocket is on. For the proxy, it shows the connected networks, open connections and traffic of each secret. For the bridge, it shows the relayed sessions and failures, and not working when the bridge cannot work. The gear button opens Settings > Telegram.

Customize in the menu at the right end of the status strip switches the panels into edit mode: Drag a panel by its handle to move it, or drop it on another panel to place the two side by side. Drag the border between two panels to change their widths. Click the eye button to hide a panel. Hidden panels are listed in the edit bar, where a click brings one back. Click Done. Reset layout returns to the default. The layout is saved in b4, so every browser shows the same one.

Reset counters in the menu at the right end of the status strip starts the counters from zero. It clears Top domains, Top addresses, the Blocked counts, the count of resets dropped by RST protection and the escalation count. It keeps the Activity history, Recent changes, the uptime, the Telegram figures, the banned addresses and the hosts escalated right now. Clear on Active Escalations sends those back.

The DPI Detector shows what the ISP does to traffic leaving the router. It finds which sites are blocked and how, whether DNS answers are forged, whether long connections to hosting networks are cut, and whether Telegram is reachable. Every site is fetched twice, directly and through b4, so the result shows both the block and whether a set fixes it. Unblocking a site shows where the detector helps. The checks and the target lists come from the dpi-detector project.

Sites to check takes domains or URLs, separated by spaces or new lines. A URL with a path is checked at that path. Without sites, the built-in list is checked. Fill from: fills the field with the built-in list, or with the domains listed by hand under Targets in the enabled sets. What to check offers four scopes: Scope What it answers Default Sites Whether each site loads, how it is blocked, and whether b4 fixes it. On DNS Whether resolvers answer blocked names honestly, whether port 53 is hijacked, and which DoH and DoT servers work. On Hosting and CDN Whether long connections to Hetzner, Cloudflare, Akamai and other networks are cut after the first kilobytes. Off Telegram Whether the datacenters are reachable, and the download and upload speed. Off Advanced holds the rest: Option What it does Default IP family IPv4, IPv6 or both. Shown while the capture engine handles both. With both, a site with an IPv6 address gets a second row. both Parallel checks How many checks run at once. A lower number is easier on a small router. 5 Fetch mode direct and through b4, or direct only. direct and through b4 Also try TLS 1.2 When a site is blocked over TLS 1.3, checks whether TLS 1.2 gets through. On Look for a working SNI on blocked hosting For each network that cuts long connections, tries known whitelisted names as the SNI. Off Run check starts the check, and Stop and keep results ends it early.

The verdict comes first, with the counts of sites blocked by the ISP, fixed by b4 and still blocked. Fix N with Discovery opens Discovery with the still-blocked sites filled in. Copy report copies a plain-text report for an issue or a forum post.

The table has a row per site, with the result Direct, the result Through b4 and the Outcome: Outcome Meaning Works Loads both ways. Fixed by b4 Blocked directly, loads through b4. The row names the set. Still blocked Blocked both ways. The row says whether no set targets the site, the set is disabled, or the set does not help. Broken by b4 Loads directly but not through b4. The matching set does harm. Site-side error The site itself answered with an error, both ways. No address from the resolver The resolver of b4's host gives no address for the site, while DoH does and the site loads at it. The direct result says how a site is blocked: Status Meaning Reset A TCP reset on the TLS handshake. Dropped The TLS handshake is never answered. Unreachable The connection is never established. Throttled The transfer stops after the first kilobytes. Fake DNS The resolver answers with a stub address. The DoH address is shown next to it. No address The resolver gives no address for the name. ISP page A redirect to, or a page from, the ISP. Fake certificate The certificate is substituted. TLS alert, Garbage reply A forged TLS alert, or injected garbage in place of TLS. Refused, Timeout The connection is refused, or nothing answers in time. Gateway The first hop in front of this host answers the connection itself, as a transparent proxy does. Nothing b4 does on this host reaches past it. Sites with Gateway or No address from the resolver have counters of their own and are left out of Fix with Discovery, since no strategy helps them. Names are resolved with the resolver of the host b4 runs on, from its /etc/resolv.conf. Devices on the network may use another resolver, so what the table shows about DNS applies to b4's host. The line above the table names the resolvers used.

The table has a row per resolver, with the resolvers of b4's host first. Latency cells show the fastest answer over UDP, DoH and DoT. Honest compares the resolver's answers for blocked names with the answers of encrypted resolvers: Value Meaning Honest The answers match. Substituted A stub or reserved address where encrypted resolvers give a real one. No answer Ordinary names resolve, while blocked names time out or return an error. Filters NXDOMAIN or an empty answer for blocked names, without a forged address. Port 53 answered by is the network that answered a query sent to the resolver. A network that is neither the provider's own nor a known public resolver marks the row as hijacked. copy DoH URL copies a working DoH server, for a set's DNS redirect.

The table has a row per network, with the number of targets cut and the point of the cut (Drops at). Working SNI, when the search was on, lists names that got through, for a set's fake SNI. Add <ASN> to a set opens the add dialog of the Traffic page with that network chosen.
The panel shows how many datacenters are reachable, and the download and upload speed.

The lists of sites, hosting targets and resolvers are built into b4 and dated. Fetch the project's current lists downloads the current lists from the dpi-detector repository and keeps them next to the configuration. Dead sites and addresses are then replaced without a b4 update. Use the built-in lists goes back to the built-in copy.
Up to fifty runs are kept with their verdict. A run can be opened again, copied as a report or deleted.

Discovery searches for a bypass strategy for the sites named in its field, or for the pages of one set. The result becomes a new set or goes into an existing one. Configured sets keep working during a run. Unblocking a site walks through a first run, and Keeping sets working shows how the watchdog runs Discovery on its own. How Discovery searches explains a run in detail.

Site or URL takes domains or full URLs, separated by commas or new lines. A domain is fetched as https://<domain>/, a URL as given. Local and private addresses are refused. Find a strategy for a set runs Discovery for one set instead and fills the field with the set's Discovery addresses, or with suggestions. A run for a set tests at most five addresses. A set that routes its traffic to a proxy or an interface cannot be picked. When another set handles an address in the field, a warning names that set. Find a strategy in a set card's menu, or on the set editor's Discovery tab, opens this page with the set picked.

The defaults are the usual choice. Option What it does Default Check DNS for tampering Compares each site's address with a trusted resolver's answer, adds a DNS fix for a forged one and looks for alternative addresses. Turning it off shortens the run when DNS is known to be clean. On Trusted DNS server The resolver the DNS check trusts, for this run only. Empty uses the one in Settings. Empty Pinned addresses Hosts-file lines, the address and then its names. Those names are tested through these addresses, and the set keeps them as pinned addresses. Empty Stop at the first strategy that works for every address Shown while a set is picked. Turned off, the search tests every strategy, which takes longer and can find a faster one. On Try community sets first Shown while the Community Hub is on. Tests up to three published sets per site before the built-in strategies. On Try strategies that worked before Winners of earlier runs go first. Forget them clears that list. On Confirm each strategy Fetches in a row a strategy has to pass during the search, 1 to 5. 1 TLS version for the probes Limits the probes, and the created set, to TLS 1.2 or 1.3. Auto IP version for the probes The same for IPv4 and IPv6. Shown while the capture engine handles both. Auto Captured ClientHello as the fake payload Fake packets carry a ClientHello captured under Settings > Payloads. None

Start begins a run through six steps: DNS, Without bypass, Strategies, Tuning, Combining and Confirming. A row per site shows what has been found so far, and Show log opens the log. A run takes from one to ten minutes, depending on the network. Stop and confirm ends the search and confirms what was found, without tuning it. Stop ends a run that has found nothing. Stop now, during the confirmation, ends the run at once and keeps the results unconfirmed. A run stops when b4 rewrites its DSCP rules during it, for example after a set's new DSCP value is saved. Its results cannot be applied, and the history marks the row stopped: firewall rules changed during the search, run it again. One run is in progress at a time, the searches of the watchdog included. A watchdog search shows on this page but cannot be stopped here.

A run for a set ends with one verdict for the whole set, above Results per address. The set's own strategy is tested first, as Current strategy of the set, and a strategy is confirmed on all addresses together. For a set with its own DSCP value, the probes carry that value, as the set's traffic does, and take the set's route through the router in front of b4. The progress and the results show DSCP <value>, as the set's traffic. The probes of any other run carry the value of Set DSCP under Settings > Core > Firewall while it is on, or none, also to the addresses of such a set. Verdict Meaning and what the card offers one strategy covers every address Apply to <set> writes the strategy into the set, see Writing into an existing set. current strategy works The set's strategy loads every address. For sites that still fail in a browser, the card names the addresses another set handles. It also notes that the browser may use QUIC (HTTP/3), which Discovery does not test, or another IP version than the run, such as IPv6. IP version for the probes sets the version a run tests. covers some addresses Apply to <set> anyway writes the best strategy. Remove them from this set's Discovery addresses drops the uncovered addresses. no bypass needed Every address loads without b4, so these pages cannot show whether the set works. nothing worked The cards below show what happened to each address. stopped before a result Nothing to apply. The set's Discovery tab shows the last run for it.

Every site gets one card, under Results per address in a run for a set. Badge Meaning and next step confirmed 3 of 3, not confirmed A strategy, a DNS fix, an alternative address or removing an ECH key made the site load. The card describes the set it creates. no bypass needed The site loads without b4. address blocked Connections to every known address fail, so no strategy can help. The site needs a VPN or a proxy. intercepted by the gateway The first hop in front of this host answers the connection itself. b4 has to run on that gateway, or this host has to be excluded from its redirect. When b4 is the router itself, only a proxy helps. does not resolve The name has no address, as with a misspelled domain. link answers 400 The link answers HTTP 400 even without b4. A link to a page or a file the site serves is needed. nothing found No strategy worked. A new run with TLS 1.2 or a captured ClientHello sometimes helps. Sites that won with the same strategy share one card and one set. N other strategies worked lists the other strategies that loaded the site, fastest first, each with Use instead. The winner is the fastest on a single fetch, which is a noisy measure: a strategy from the list is as valid a choice.

Apply as a set, Apply in the history and Use instead open one dialog. It previews the set and offers: Create a new set, then Create set: see Creating a set. Write the strategy into an existing set, then Replace strategy: see below. This is the default when the run was for a set or a set lists the site exactly. Add to <set>, which already uses the same strategy, then Add to set: adds the sites to that set. When the set's strategy changed after the dialog opened, nothing is added. Copy JSON copies the set without creating it, in the Import/Export format. A result is applied only to a set whose traffic takes the network path the run tested: the DSCP value of the run's probes, written on the same interfaces. A change to the set's DSCP value, to Set DSCP or to its interface list after the run can change that path. The error then names the difference, and a new run for the set tests the new path. For a few seconds after such a change is saved, while b4 applies its DSCP rules, applying and starting a run are refused.

Which set to change lists the run's set and the enabled sets without routing that already match the site. Another set picks any other set without routing. Only the bypass strategy is written: TCP, fragmentation, fake packets and, when the result uses them, a DNS redirect, pinned addresses and removing ECH keys. The port filter, RST protection, UDP, targets, routing and escalation stay as they are. Use these addresses as the set's discovery URLs also replaces the set's Discovery addresses. When the set does not match the sites, Add <sites> to this set adds them and moves them out of other enabled sets. The dialog warns when another set actually handles a site, since the new strategy has no effect there.

The suggested Set name is the site without its prefix and top-level domain. Match can shorten a single site to a parent domain, so the set also covers its subdomains. A site listed in another enabled set moves into the new one. The new set goes to the top of the list, enabled. It gets a DNS redirect or pinned addresses only for a site that needed them. The tested addresses become its Discovery addresses, so the set can be searched again or watched.

Some blocks hand out an address that refuses every connection, while clients in other regions get addresses that work. With Check DNS for tampering on, Discovery looks for such addresses when every known address of a site fails. The set pins the site's name to up to three addresses that complete a TLS handshake, so devices get those in DNS answers. The pins are fixed at the time of the run. When the block moves, a new run with the DNS check on finds new ones. Watchdog searches skip the DNS check and do not refresh pins.

A site that publishes an ECH key is probed the way a browser with the key connects, so the ClientHello names the key's public name, such as cloudflare-ech.com. The set targets that name as well. When the network drops ClientHellos with ECH and the site loads without it, the card is marked ECH blocked. The result is ECH keys removed: a set that turns on Remove ECH keys from DNS answers and changes no packets. A browser with its own secure DNS still sends ECH, so it needs one of the other strategies listed under the result.

The history keeps the latest result of each site, newest first. Apply creates the set the run built, without a new run. Run again repeats the run for the site, or for the set the row came from. Remove from history and Clear history remove one row or all of them. A row expands to the other strategies that worked, each with Use instead. Tried marks a strategy that has been applied as a set, also after the set is deleted. via watchdog and via MCP mark runs that the watchdog or an AI assistant over MCP started. Last run log opens the log of the last run, also after a restart, and can download it as a text file.

A set can answer DNS for the domains it targets: send them to another resolver, answer them with fixed addresses, or remove parts of the answers. Names that no set targets go to the resolver the device chose, unchanged. The options are on the set's DNS & Routing tab, under DNS Redirect, see DNS & Routing.

b4 sees DNS that goes to port 53, from the devices on the network and from the router itself. Encrypted DNS that a device sends by itself (DoH, DoT or DoQ) passes b4 unseen, and the sets do not apply to it. The usual sources are secure DNS in a browser such as Chrome or Firefox, Android Private DNS, and a DoH resolver set up on the device. The sets apply to such a device once encrypted DNS is turned off on it. An encrypted forwarder on the router is not a problem, since devices still ask the router on port 53. The interception itself is described in How b4 handles DNS.

A query name matches a set the way a server name does: a domain covers its subdomains, and a domain listed in one set wins over a regexp: entry in another. A block set answers first, then the set's pins, then the set's resolver while Enable DNS Redirect is on. Otherwise the query goes to the device's resolver unchanged. b4 can then remove ECH keys and IPv6 addresses from the answer, see the full sequence.
documents.s: How a set handles a query

documents.t: A set's resolver helps when the provider's DNS answers the set's domains with wrong addresses. Open Sets and open the set. On the DNS & Routing tab, under DNS Redirect, turn on Enable DNS Redirect. Under Resolver type, choose Plain DNS (UDP) and a DNS Server IP, or DNS-over-HTTPS and a DNS-over-HTTPS URL, typed in or picked from the recommended list. Click Save Changes. Resolver type When it fits Plain DNS (UDP) Plain DNS to other servers arrives intact. Fragment DNS Queries splits each query into IP fragments, for DPI that reads the names in DNS queries. DNS-over-HTTPS The provider tampers with plain DNS to other servers too, or the resolver serves only DoH. The queries leave encrypted. Queries from the set's own resolver go on unchanged, so a resolver on the local network can serve a set. A resolver on the router itself has one more condition, see When it does not work. A service that checks the address a connection comes from needs another exit rather than another resolver, see Routing sites through a VPN.
documents.s: Sending a set's domains to another resolver

documents.t: When b4 looks up a set's names itself, for routing, a DSCP value or a proxy upstream, it uses the set's resolver while Enable DNS Redirect is on, and the router's resolver otherwise, see How b4 handles DNS.

When the set's resolver does not answer, b4 answers from the last good reply it holds for the name, or else asks the resolver the device was addressing. Query timeout under Settings > Core > DNS sets how long b4 waits. Fail closed when the resolver is unreachable turns the fallback off. The device then gets an error (SERVFAIL), and the set's names resolve through its resolver or not at all. warning With fail closed on, an unreachable resolver stops every name of the set from resolving, even while the bypass strategy works. On a censored connection, the DoH server itself can get blocked.

A pin answers a name with fixed addresses, with no hosts file to edit on every device. It helps when DNS keeps handing out an address that does not answer. Domain and addresses under Pinned addresses takes hosts file lines, one per address: the address first, then the names it answers for. 157.240.0.174 www.instagram.com 157.240.205.63 scontent.cdninstagram.com scontent-a.cdninstagram.com A pin covers each name and its subdomains. The longest matching entry wins. A pin applies only to a name the set targets. For other names the editor offers Add to this set's domains. Pins work with Enable DNS Redirect off too, and win over the set's resolver. The pins are the whole address answer: a name pinned to IPv4 addresses only gets no IPv6 addresses. In a set without routing, b4 leaves out pinned addresses that do not answer on TCP port 443, checked at start, on save and at the Retest interval (seconds) of IP Block Detection. When none answers, the pins are used anyway.

While Enable IPv6 Support is off, b4 processes IPv4 only, and a site with IPv6 addresses would be reached over IPv6, past every set. b4 therefore removes the IPv6 addresses (AAAA records) from the answers for names a set matches, and the device connects over IPv4. Other names keep their full answers. The switch is Force IPv4 for matched domains on the IPv4 / IPv6 card under Settings > Core > Packet Engine. It is on by default and unused while Enable IPv6 Support is on. A set limited to IPv6 by its IP Version Filter keeps its IPv6 answers. An address the device already has from its cache, a hosts file or its own encrypted DNS still leads over IPv6. Enable IPv6 Support closes that path.

Sites behind some CDNs publish an Encrypted ClientHello (ECH) key in DNS. A browser that gets the key, such as Chrome, sends a ClientHello that names the CDN's shared name instead of the site: cloudflare-ech.com for every Cloudflare site. Where DPI drops such ClientHellos, all these sites stop loading at once. Remove ECH keys from DNS answers, under Encrypted ClientHello (ECH), takes the key out, and the browser sends an ordinary ClientHello naming the site. It works with Enable DNS Redirect off too. The key is removed when: the name asked matches the set, such as steamdb.info listed in the set; the key's public name is a domain the set matches. A set listing cloudflare-ech.com removes the key from every Cloudflare site's answers. While Enable IPv6 Support is off, b4 in NFQUEUE mode also removes the key from answers that arrive over IPv6. A set that uses Source Devices leaves such answers alone, since b4 cannot tell which device they go to. A device added by hand by its IPv6 address is the exception. Discovery proposes such a set, with no packet changes, for a site that loads without ECH but not with it. A key already in a browser's cache is used until it expires.

A set that targets every name sends the DNS of the whole network and of the router to one DoH resolver. Domains listed in other sets keep their own sets' resolvers. Open Sets and click Create Set. On the Import/Export tab, paste the configuration below into Set Configuration JSON and click Import. To use another resolver, change DNS-over-HTTPS URL on the DNS & Routing tab. Click Create Set. { "b4_version": "dev", "name": "all DOH", "tcp": { "dport_filter": "53" }, "udp": { "dport_filter": "53" }, "fragmentation": { "strategy": "none" }, "faking": { "sni": false }, "targets": { "sni_domains": ["regexp:.*"] }, "enabled": true, "dns": { "enabled": true, "doh_url": "https://wikimedia-dns.org/dns-query" } } The set changes no packets, and its port filters of 53 keep it off TLS and QUIC connections. Router host names and .lan names stop resolving, since the public resolver does not know them; pins keep the ones that matter working. When the resolver is unreachable, every name falls back, so a resolver reachable from the connection matters more than its features.
documents.s: Sending every DNS query to DoH

documents.t: Settings > Core > DNS holds the interception of DNS over TCP and the timeouts for all sets. Without Intercept DNS over TCP, a device that retries a query over TCP reaches its own resolver, past the set.

Open Traffic. Enter flags:dns in the filter to keep only DNS queries. Open a site of the set on a device. Each query shows the set that matched it and a label: Label Meaning doh <server>, forward <address> Resolved through the set's DoH or plain DNS server pin, pin empty Answered from the pins, empty when they hold no address of the type asked ipv4 only, no ech IPv6 addresses or the ECH key removed from the answer heal, heal + ipv4 only Unreachable addresses removed or replaced by Heal DNS answers, or banned addresses removed or replaced sinkhole, block A block set answered "does not exist" or dropped the query fallback-cache, fallback-upstream The set's resolver did not answer: the last good reply was used, or the device's resolver answered servfail The set's resolver did not answer and nothing else could, or the set fails closed passthrough, bad target, from target, ipv6 off Passed on unchanged: the set has no resolver, DNS Server IP is not a valid address, the query came from the set's own resolver, or it came over IPv6 while IPv6 support is off escalate <set> Lookups for the name kept failing, and the backup set of Escalation answered The log records the same decisions, as dns-doh->, dns-pin and so on. Both show DNS decisions while Log Level is Info, the default, or more detailed.

What happens Cause and fix A device's lookups never show on the Traffic page The device uses encrypted DNS. Turning off secure DNS in its browser, or Android Private DNS, sends its lookups to the router. The site still goes to the old address The device keeps an answer it already has until the answer expires. servfail, fallback-cache or fallback-upstream The set's resolver is unreachable from this connection. Another resolver, or DoH in place of plain DNS, is the next try. The set's names resolve slowly or not at all, with the set's resolver on the router A resolver on the router, and the router's resolver when a resolver on the network uses it upstream, has to reach its own upstream over DoH or DoT, which b4 does not intercept. A browser still uses ECH, with a resolver on the network that checks DNSSEC, such as BIND or Unbound The resolver gets the original answer on a path b4 does not see: DoT or DoH to its upstream, an interface left out of Capture Interfaces, or TCP while Intercept DNS over TCP is off. With Intercept DNS over TCP on, plain DNS through a captured interface closes these paths, see ECH keys.

On KeeneticOS and some other routers with an older kernel, b4 works on copies of DNS requests and replaces the resolver's reply with the set's answer. The row DNS queries copied, not held (NFLOG) in System Info shows when. The resolver the device asked then still receives every request, and a resolver outside the router has to reply before the device gets the set's answer. Requests that a nat rule moves to another port, or that NAT sends from another source port, get no set handling, see Copied requests.
A set acts only on the traffic its targets name. Sites are added on the set's Targets tab, or with the + buttons on the Traffic page and the dashboard, which add one domain or address at a time.
A set to add the sites to. The + buttons can create one as well. For GeoSite and GeoIP categories, the databases loaded under Settings > Geodat Settings.

Target Use it for Sub-tab Domain A site reached by name, which is most sites. A domain covers its subdomains, so a service that serves content from many subdomains is covered by its parent domain, such as googlevideo.com for YouTube. Bypass Domains GeoSite category A ready-made list of a service's domains, such as youtube or discord. Bypass Domains IP address or range Connections made straight to an address, without a name, such as those of Telegram apps, voice calls or games. Bypass IPs GeoIP category The address ranges of a country or a network, from the GeoIP database. Bypass IPs ASN Every address range a network announces, kept up to date by b4. A cloud, hosting or CDN network also carries many unrelated sites. ASN

Open Sets and click the set's card. On the Targets tab, open Bypass Domains, type a domain into Add Bypass Domain and press Enter. Several domains can be pasted at once, separated by commas or new lines. For a GeoSite category, pick it under Add Bypass Category. For addresses, open Bypass IPs and use Add Bypass IP/CIDR or Add Bypass GeoIP Category. For a network, open ASN and enter its number, such as AS15169, or an IP address of the service. For an address, b4 offers the networks that announce it. Click Save Changes. Targets describes every field of the tab.

The Traffic page lists the connections b4 sees, and the dashboard's Top domains and addresses panels list the names and addresses that devices use most. A + next to a name or an address opens a dialog that adds it to a set. On the dashboard, + marks the names and addresses that no set matched. For a domain: Click + next to the domain. Pick the pattern: the domain itself or one of its parent domains. A parent domain covers every subdomain. Under Target Set, pick a set, or Create New Set and enter its name. Click Add Domain. For an address: Click + next to the address. The dialog looks up the network that announces it. Under What to add, pick the address alone, the announced prefix that covers it, a broader mask, or the whole network, its ASN. Under Target Set, pick a set or create one. Click the button that names what is added, such as Add 142.250.120.139 or Add AS15169. Adding domains to sets and Adding addresses and networks to sets describe both dialogs. The DPI Detector opens the address dialog from its Hosting and CDN results.
documents.s: Adding from the Traffic page or the dashboard

documents.t: The set's card on the Sets page shows the new targets. An ASN whose prefixes are not fetched yet shows as N ASN unresolved. On the Traffic page and the dashboard, the next connections to the site carry the set's badge. The dashboard's Sets panel counts the connections the set matched.

The connections carry another set's badge. Another set targets the same site and takes its connections, for example a set limited to the device. When a domain is already in another set, the Targets tab names that set. How sets match traffic describes how b4 chooses. The connections carry no set at all. The set may be turned off, or the site may load from other domains. The Traffic page shows the names it really uses, and Domains not in any set on the dashboard opens it with only the connections no set matched. A category or an ASN adds nothing. The GeoSite or GeoIP database is not loaded, or the ASN's prefixes could not be fetched yet. b4 retries an ASN in the background. The site is matched but still does not open. The set's strategy does not work for it, see Unblocking a site.

By default b4 handles the traffic of every device on the network. Device filtering under Settings > Core > Devices decides which devices get DPI bypass at all. The Source Devices of a set limit that one set to some devices.
The devices are on the router's network, where b4 finds them in the ARP table. A device behind another router has a fixed or reserved IP address, since it can be added only by that address.

Open Settings > Core > Devices. Turn on Enable Device Filtering. Under Available Devices, select the devices. A device missing from the list is added under Manual Devices by its IP address. To exclude the selected devices instead of limiting DPI bypass to them, turn on Exclude Selected Devices (Blacklist). Click Save Changes, then Restart Service. The selection applies after a restart. What the filter covers: DPI bypass matches devices by MAC address. A device added by hand does not count for it, and a selection made only of such devices leaves DPI bypass on for every device. Routing sets and Telegram over WebSocket use the same selection for traffic from the network. There a device added by hand is matched by its IP address. The router itself is not a device. Its own connections, those of the SOCKS5 proxy included, get DPI bypass in both modes. While devices are selected, sets do not write their own DSCP value. The fields are described under Devices.
documents.s: Choosing the devices that get DPI bypass

documents.t: Open the set, then Targets > Source Devices. Select the devices. To apply the set to every device except the selected ones, turn on All devices except selected. Save the set. A set limited to source devices takes priority over a set without that limit. Source devices narrow whom a set applies to, but they do not select traffic. A routing set still needs a domain, IP or ASN target, and Match any IP address under Bypass IPs routes everything from those devices. See Source devices.
documents.s: Applying one set to some devices

documents.t: Open Traffic. In the Devices panel, select a device. Its connections show the set that matched each of them. Devices that device filtering leaves out get no DPI bypass, and the dashboard does not count their connections.

Nothing changed after saving. The device filter applies after a restart of b4. A device added by hand gets no DPI bypass. DPI bypass matches MAC addresses only. Such a device can still be the source device of a set. A device added by hand is not matched. Its IP address changed, or a router in between replaces the source address of its traffic. The first needs a fixed or reserved address; the second cannot be matched at all. A phone stops being matched. Many phones use a randomized MAC address, shown as Private, and a new address is a new device for b4. Turning off the private address for this network on the phone keeps its MAC address fixed. A device that is gone stays in the list as offline. b4 keeps a device's name, selection and MSS value until the device is forgotten under Available Devices. A replacement device, or a phone with a new random MAC address, is a new device and needs its own selection.

The setup adds a set that sends fakes before the UDP packets that open a Discord voice call. It is needed when a call sends its voice packets but gets no answer, or drops after a few seconds, while the rest of Discord works. A call that hangs at RTC Connecting fails on TCP instead, see When it does not work. The address of a voice server is not known in advance. The set therefore has no targets and handles only calls on the voice ports, see Sets for calls. Once it takes the packet that opens a call, the rest of that call belongs to the set and passes untouched, whatever other sets match its address.

b4 is installed and running. A set that already opens Discord itself, the app and text chat. Adding sites to a set adds Discord's domains to a set, and The Discord set's TCP ports lists the ports that set needs.

Open Sets and click Create Set. Enter a name for the set, such as Discord voice. Leave the Targets tab empty. On the UDP tab, in Calls, select Handle only calls. Which calls stays at Discord app and browsers, and a warning asks for a port filter. Click Use Discord ports in the warning, or enter 19294-19344,50000-50100 in Port Filter. Leave Action Mode at Fake & Fragment. Fake Packet Payload now shows (auto: STUN request). On the TCP tab, leave Port Filter under General empty. Click Create Set. Ports Voice servers 19294-19344 Discord's voice servers on Cloudflare 50000-50100 The other voice servers, for example in Finland With Discord app and browsers, the set takes calls and voice channels in the Discord app, and calls in a browser, Discord in a browser included. Fake Packet Count and Fake Packet Size keep their defaults.

The JSON below creates the same set without the steps above. Settings it leaves out keep their defaults. { "name": "Discord voice", "udp": { "dport_filter": "19294-19344,50000-50100", "filter_l7": ["discord", "stun"], "fake_payload_file": "@stun" } } Open Sets and click Create Set. Go to the Import/Export tab, paste the JSON into Set Configuration JSON and click Import. Click Create Set. The Community Hub can carry a set of this kind as well. A zapret line for Discord voice with no host list or ipset of its own, such as --filter-udp=19294-19344,50000-50100 --filter-l7=discord,stun --dpi-desync=fake, converts into the same set on import.

The Discord app, text chat and the signalling connection of a call run over TCP. They belong to the set with Discord's domains: the GeoSite category discord, or domains such as discord.com, discord.gg and discord.media. b4 captures TCP port 443 and the ports that any set lists. Discord's other TCP ports therefore have to be in that set's list. Open the set with Discord's domains. On the TCP tab, enter 443,2053,2083,2087,2096,8443 in Port Filter under General. Click Save Changes. The list limits the set to these ports, and 443 keeps it on HTTPS. The voice server picks one of these ports for the signalling connection of a call, and the set's strategy has to work on each of them. A strategy that opens discord.com on port 443 can still fail on the port of a voice server, and Checking the voice server tests that port. The watchdog checks a new strategy only on the set's Discovery addresses, and an address given as a domain is checked on port 443. A strategy it writes can then open Discord and break calls, so keeping the watchdog off for this set is the usual choice.

Join a voice channel in Discord. Open the Traffic page. Turn on All packets. Voice packets carry no domain and show only with it on. Switch to Raw feed in the top right corner. The packet that opens the voice connection and the STUN requests show the voice set's name in the Set column, with a destination port from the two ranges. The packets that follow on the same connection show the voice set as well, with a voice label: the set passed them through untouched.

Before the first voice packet, Discord opens a TCP connection to the voice server. Its domain ends in discord.media, and its port is one of the ports in The Discord set's TCP ports. Join a voice channel in Discord. On the Traffic page, switch to Raw feed and enter domain:discord.media in the filter field. Note the domain of the latest row, such as c-xxx.discord.media, and the port in its destination. On a computer behind the router, run the command below with that domain and port. curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}/%{size_download}\n' https://c-xxx.discord.media:2087/ Output Meaning 403 and a few thousand bytes, such as 403/4548 The server's answer passes. 000/0 or 403/0 The connection to this port is cut.

While a call hangs, the Traffic page with All packets on shows which side fails. The Traffic page shows Cause No TCP row with a discord.media domain b4 does not capture the voice server's port: it is missing from the Port Filter of the set with Discord's domains. A TCP row with a discord.media domain, and no UDP packet to the voice ports The TCP connection to the voice server fails, and Discord sends no voice packet. Checking the voice server confirms it, and the set with Discord's domains needs a strategy that works on that port, see Unblocking a site. UDP packets to the voice ports with the voice set's name The voice server does not answer them, see the causes below. On some networks no strategy opens the voice server's port when it is not 443. The check then reads 000/0 whatever the strategy, and calls through that server need a proxy or a VPN for discord.media. b4 refuses to save the voice set. A warning on the UDP tab names the cause: the set has targets, its Port Filter is empty, or the TCP tab lists ports. The set saves with no targets, both port ranges in the UDP Port Filter and an empty TCP Port Filter. No packet to the voice ports shows the voice set. The voice set took neither the packet that opens the call nor the STUN requests. Their port is missing from its Port Filter, Which calls leaves that kind of call out, or the set is turned off on the Sets page. The IP Version Filter on the set's Targets tab can also exclude one IP version. No packets to the voice ports appear. All packets is off, or the port is missing from the voice set's Port Filter: b4 sees UDP only on port 443 and on the ports that sets list. With Enable IPv6 Support off under Settings > Core, b4 sees no IPv6 packets at all. Calls through one Discord server fail, and calls through other servers work. A voice channel uses the region Discord picks automatically. When a provider blocks the addresses of that region's voice servers, no strategy helps. Someone who can manage the voice channel sets another region for it in the channel's settings in Discord. The voice server check passes over IPv4 and fails over IPv6. With the TTL strategy, or with Apply Fake TTL on, the set with Discord's domains sends its fakes with one Fake TTL for IPv4 and IPv6. A voice server can be fewer hops away over IPv6, and a fake that reaches the server breaks the connection. A lower Fake TTL on the Faking sub-tab, checked over both IP versions, is the fix. Discord does not open at all. The set with Discord's domains does not cover the TCP side. Its Port Filter needs the ports from The Discord set's TCP ports, and its strategy has to open Discord, see Unblocking a site.

A set can write a DSCP value of its own into the packets sent to the set's addresses. DSCP is a field of the IP header, so the value leaves the host with the packet. The router in front of b4 tells the set's traffic apart by it and sends it, after b4 has processed it, through a route of its own, such as a VPN or a second uplink. b4 itself does not route by the value.

A router in front of b4 that can match DSCP and route by a connection mark, such as Linux with nftables or RouterOS. b4 installs its firewall rules: Skip IPTables/NFTables Setup under Settings > Core > Firewall is off. With iptables, the ipset command and the xt_set and xt_DSCP kernel modules are present; on OpenWrt xt_DSCP comes with kmod-ipt-ipopt and iptables-mod-ipopt. A set with routing off or in Network interface mode, with no source devices and no source interfaces. When the value is not written lists every case. Device Filtering under Settings > Core > Devices off, or on with no device selected. While it has a device selected, in either mode, no set writes its value; Set DSCP still applies.

Open Sets, open the set, then DNS & Routing > Traffic Routing. In the DSCP block at the bottom, turn on Enable per-set DSCP. b4 fills in DSCP value with the first of 7, 31, 6 and 25 that no other set and no Set DSCP uses. Click Save Changes. Optionally, turn on Set DSCP under Settings > Core > Firewall. It writes its own value into every other packet, so no device whose traffic passes through b4 can pick the set's route by writing the set's value itself. Each route needs a value of its own. The field is described under DSCP.

Every device on the path sees the value until something resets it, and some act on it. Linux Wi-Fi drivers, and access points that follow the same mapping, pick the WMM queue from it: Values Wi-Fi queue 7, 31, 6, 25 Best effort, as for traffic without a value 8 and several other values below 24 Background 32-63, and from Linux 6.8 on 24, 26, 28 and 30 Video and voice 7, 31, 6 and 25 keep normal priority in cake and pfifo_fast as well. The hint under DSCP value lists where the other values land, and Choosing the value gives the values for pfSense.

The router in front of b4 has to: Decide on the first packet of a connection and keep the decision, with a connection mark. Routing each packet by its own field moves a connection to another route when the value appears in the middle of it, and behind NAT that breaks the connection. With flow offloading on b4's host, such as an nftables flowtable, FLOWOFFLOAD or hardware NAT, only the first packets of a connection carry the value. Compare the whole field. nftables ip dscp and RouterOS dscp= compare all six bits. The tos selector of ip rule compares only some of them for IPv4: to it, 7, 15, 31 and 63 look the same. Reset the field on the internet uplink and on the tunnel, so the provider and the far end of the tunnel do not see it. A reset in the forwarding path misses the packets that FastTrack, an nftables flowtable or hardware NAT carries past it. Accept the value only from b4, by its address or MAC address. Devices whose traffic passes through b4 are kept out only by Set DSCP on b4. Let in the replies of the second route. Strict reverse-path filtering, Linux rp_filter 1 or RouterOS rp-filter=strict, drops them. While b4 is stopped, restarting or running without its packet engine, new connections carry no value and take the main route. A router that uses the Set DSCP value to keep b4's traffic out of a route leading to b4 sends that traffic back to b4 meanwhile; a match on the interface or the MAC address does not depend on b4 running.
documents.s: Reading the value on the next router

documents.t: One nftables table reads the value. In the example the router reaches b4 through br-lan, the main uplink is wan, the second route is the uplink wanb, and the set's value is 31. The table goes into a file such as /etc/dscp_route.nft, loaded with nft -f /etc/dscp_route.nft; loading it again replaces the table. table inet dscp_route delete table inet dscp_route table inet dscp_route { chain prerouting { type filter hook prerouting priority mangle; policy accept; iifname "br-lan" ip saddr 192.168.50.2 ct state new ct status & confirmed == 0 ip dscp 31 ct mark set ct mark | 0x01000000 iifname "br-lan" ip6 saddr { fd50::2, fd10::/64 } ct state new ct status & confirmed == 0 ip6 dscp 31 ct mark set ct mark | 0x01000000 iifname "br-lan" ct mark & 0x01000000 == 0x01000000 meta mark set meta mark | 0x01000000 } chain postrouting { type filter hook postrouting priority mangle; policy accept; oifname { "wan", "wanb" } ip dscp != 0 ip dscp set 0 oifname { "wan", "wanb" } ip6 dscp != 0 ip6 dscp set 0 } chain srcnat { type nat hook postrouting priority srcnat; policy accept; oifname { "wan", "wanb" } masquerade } } The marked connections take routing table 100, whose default route leads out of wanb: ip rule add fwmark 0x1000000/0x1000000 iif br-lan lookup 100 priority 1000 ip route add default via 100.64.2.1 dev wanb table 100 ip -6 rule add fwmark 0x1000000/0x1000000 iif br-lan lookup 100 priority 1000 ip -6 route add default via 2001:db8:b::1 dev wanb table 100 The ip applet of busybox 1.37 takes the same lines. Neither the table nor these commands survive a reboot by themselves; they belong in the router's startup scripts. In the example Stands for br-lan The kernel device name of the interface toward b4, not OpenWrt's interface name 192.168.50.2 b4's IPv4 address, best fixed with a static lease. Forwarded IPv4 traffic carries it only while Enable NAT Masquerade is on in b4 (NAT Masquerade); without it, the subnet behind b4 joins it: ip saddr { 192.168.50.2, <subnet> } fd50::2, fd10::/64 b4's own IPv6 address and the IPv6 prefix of the devices behind b4. The line is left out when no IPv6 passes through b4 31 The set's value. Each further value needs its own pair of marking lines 0x01000000 A bit of the connection mark and the packet mark that nothing else on the router uses. A further route takes another bit and another table 100, 1000 The table of the second uplink, and a free rule priority below the main table's 32766 and ahead of other policy rules 100.64.2.1, 2001:db8:b::1 The gateways of the second uplink Chain srcnat Masquerading on both uplinks, which the router's own firewall may already do ct status & confirmed == 0 matches only the packet that creates the connection; ct state new alone also matches a repeated SYN and moves the connection in the middle. nft 1.0.2 and later print it as ct status ! confirmed, which nft 0.9.8 does not accept.
